Forefront Content:
What is an ERP system?

Before answering whether Colleague fits the category, it helps to define the category itself. An enterprise resource planning (ERP) system is a centralized software platform that unifies an organization's core operational functions—finance, human resources, procurement, payroll, and reporting—around a single shared database. Instead of running disconnected tools that don't talk to each other, an ERP lets every department pull from the same source of truth. In higher education, the definition stretches further: an ERP also has to manage student records, admissions, registration, financial aid, and billing. That's a wider footprint than most corporate ERPs carry, which is exactly why the higher-ed market developed purpose-built platforms of its own.

‍

Is colleague an ERP system?

Is colleague an ERP system? Yes. Ellucian Colleague is a full enterprise resource planning (ERP) system designed specifically for colleges and universities. It ties together the academic and administrative sides of an institution—student information, finance, human resources, payroll, and financial aid—inside one integrated environment. Some people call it a student information system (SIS), and that label isn't wrong, but it's incomplete. The SIS functions are one part of a broader ERP. So when someone asks whether Colleague is considered an ERP, the accurate answer is that it's an ERP that happens to include a robust SIS at its core, along with the back-office modules an institution needs to run finance and HR operations.

‍

What does Colleague do for colleges and universities?

Colleague earns its ERP designation by consolidating the systems that used to live in separate silos. Its core capabilities typically include:

  • Student: admissions, registration, academic records, degree audit, and retention tracking.
  • Finance: general ledger, accounts payable and receivable, budgeting, and procurement.
  • Human Resources and Payroll: position management, benefits, time entry, and payroll processing.
  • Financial Aid: packaging, disbursement, and federal compliance reporting.
  • Reporting and analytics: institution-wide dashboards drawn from a shared data model.

Because these modules share one database, a change in a student's enrollment status can flow automatically to billing and financial aid without manual re-entry. That interconnection is the defining trait of an enterprise resource planning system, and it's where the operational value—fewer redundancies, cleaner data, faster reporting—actually comes from. It unifies information across departments, so finance, human resources, financial aid, and student records all draw from the same up-to-date source.

‍

How does Colleague compare to Banner and Anthology?

Colleague isn't the only higher-education ERP in the Ellucian family, and the distinction matters when leaders evaluate their roadmap. Banner is Ellucian's other flagship ERP, historically favored by larger and more complex institutions with heavy customization needs, while Colleague has long been the platform of choice for community colleges, private institutions, and mid-sized universities that value a more streamlined, out-of-the-box configuration. For a closer side-by-side look at the two platforms, see What is the difference between Ellucian Banner and colleague? Anthology's SIS and ERP business joined the Ellucian family following Anthology's Chapter 11 restructuring, so institutions that once weighed Anthology as a separate ERP option are now evaluating it as part of the broader Ellucian portfolio. The practical takeaway is that "Is Colleague an enterprise resource planning system?" and "Which ERP is right for us?" are two different questions. Confirming that Colleague qualifies as an ERP is easy; deciding how to configure, integrate, and optimize it around your institution's specific goals is the harder work.

Owning an ERP and getting full value from one are not the same thing. Many institutions run Colleague for years without ever optimizing configurations, retiring shadow systems, or connecting it cleanly to the CRMs, learning platforms, and reporting tools that surround it. That gap between a capable platform and its real-world performance is where expertise pays off. The teams that get the most out of their ERP tend to do a few things well:

Forefront Content:
What Ellucian Colleague actually does

Colleague is an enterprise resource planning (ERP) system built specifically for higher education—more precisely, a student information system (SIS) at its core. It serves as the system of record for the data your institution depends on every day:

  • Student records, registration, and academic history
  • Financial aid packaging and disbursement
  • Student accounts, billing, and receivables
  • Human resources, payroll, and finance
  • Curriculum, course catalogs, and degree audit

In other words, it manages transactions and records. Colleague is the authoritative source that keeps your institution running and compliant—a fundamentally different job than nurturing relationships.

‍

So, is it a CRM?

No—Colleague is built as the institution's system of record, not a relationship-management platform, which is why most community colleges pair it with a dedicated recruitment and enrollment CRM to run the front end of the funnel. A CRM (customer relationship management) platform is designed to manage relationships and communications across a person's lifecycle—tracking outreach, engagement, and the many touchpoints that move a prospect toward enrollment or an alum toward giving. The SIS, by contrast, is transactional. It records what happened; a CRM orchestrates what happens next. So when teams ask whether Colleague is a CRM, they're usually sensing a real gap: the system holds rich data but wasn't built for marketing automation, lead scoring, or multi-channel campaign management.

‍

CRM vs. student information system: what's the difference?

The distinction comes down to purpose. A student information system is your operational backbone, while a CRM is your engagement engine. Here's how they compare:

  • Primary role: An SIS stores official records; a CRM manages relationships and communications.
  • Data focus: An SIS tracks enrollment, grades, and financials; a CRM tracks inquiries, interactions, and behaviors.
  • Users: Registrars, financial aid, and business offices live in the SIS; recruiters, advisors, and advancement teams live in the CRM.
  • Lifecycle stage: A CRM works the funnel before and around enrollment; the SIS governs the record once a student is active.

Ellucian actually offers dedicated CRM products—for recruiting, advising, and advancement—precisely because these functions sit outside what the SIS was designed to do. Treating your record system as a CRM usually leads to clunky workarounds, poor communication tracking, and frustrated staff.

‍

How Colleague and a CRM work together

The real value emerges when your SIS and CRM share data cleanly. A recruit's inquiry lives in the CRM, and once they enroll, that record flows into the system of record as the official source. Done well, integration eliminates duplicate data entry and gives every team a consistent view of each constituent. For deeper guidance on this integration strategy, see How easy is it to integrate Ellucian Colleague with other campus technologies like learning management systems? A practical approach looks like this:

  1. Define which system owns which data and when—clear data governance prevents the two platforms from fighting over the "truth."
  2. Map the fields and lifecycle triggers that move a person from prospect to enrolled student.
  3. Build reliable, secure integrations rather than manual exports, protecting sensitive records under FERPA and related standards.
  4. Establish reporting that draws from both systems so leaders see the full picture, from first touch to degree completion.

When institutions skip these steps, they end up with two disconnected systems and a fractured constituent experience—the opposite of what they hoped to achieve.

Making the right technology decision

Name: Can Ellucian Colleague be customized to fit the unique needs of different colleges or universities?
Short Description: Can Ellucian Colleague be customized to fit the unique needs of different colleges or universities? It's one of the first questions leaders ask when they evaluate their student information system against the reality of how their campus actually operates. Every institution carries its own degree structures, registration rules, financial aid logic, and reporting demands—no two are identical. The good news is that this platform was built with that variability in mind, and the answer is a confident yes, with a caveat: how you customize matters as much as whether you can.
Forefront Content:
What can actually be customized in your student information system?

Flexibility here shows up in layers, from light configuration to deeper engineering. Institutions routinely tailor the environment without ever touching source code, then extend further when a genuine business need calls for it. Common areas where colleges shape the system to fit their needs include:

  • Configuration and parameters — turning delivered functionality on or off, defining academic calendars, term structures, grading schemes, and workflow rules that mirror your policies.
  • Custom fields and screens — capturing institution-specific data points on constituents, courses, or applications that the delivered design doesn't track by default.
  • Reporting and analytics — building custom reports, dashboards, and extracts so registrars, finance, and enrollment teams see the metrics they actually manage against.
  • Integrations — connecting the platform to your learning management system, CRM, payment processors, and third-party tools so data flows cleanly instead of living in silos. For a deeper look at how these connections work, see How easy is it to integrate Ellucian Colleague with other campus technologies like learning management systems?
  • Portal and self-service experiences — adjusting the student- and faculty-facing interface so the digital experience reflects your brand and simplifies the tasks people perform most.
  • Custom code and subroutines — when a requirement can't be met through configuration, purpose-built logic can extend behavior for a unique process.

Because Colleague serves community colleges, small privates, and large multi-campus systems alike, this range is deliberate. A two-year college with open enrollment and a research university with complex prerequisite chains can both bend the same platform to fit their needs—just through different combinations of these levers.

‍

How much customization is too much?

The ability to change almost anything doesn't mean you should. The most expensive lesson institutions learn is that heavy custom code creates technical debt: every upgrade, patch, and vendor enhancement now has to be tested against modifications the vendor never anticipated. Over years, that turns routine maintenance into risky, resource-draining projects and can quietly trap a campus on an aging release. The healthier discipline is to exhaust configuration first, treat custom development as the exception rather than the reflex, and document every deviation from delivered functionality. Ask a simple question of each request: does this reflect a real institutional differentiator—a genuinely unique way we serve students—or are we recreating a process the platform already supports because "that's how we've always done it"? Modernization efforts often reveal that a surprising share of "must-have" customizations are legacy habits rather than requirements. Cutting those loose lowers cost, shortens upgrade cycles, and protects the very flexibility you paid for.

‍

Building a customization strategy that lasts

Knowing that a system can be tailored to fit the unique needs of different colleges is only half the work; deciding how is where value is won or lost. A durable approach usually follows a clear sequence:

  1. Assess before you build. Inventory current customizations, map them to active business processes, and separate what drives outcomes from what drives overhead.
  2. Standardize where you can. Adopt delivered functionality and configuration wherever it meets the need, reserving engineering effort for true differentiators.
  3. Govern the requests. Put decision rights, documentation standards, and change management in place so new customizations are approved deliberately, not accumulated by default.
  4. Design for upgradability. Structure integrations and any custom code so future releases, security patches, and enhancements can be absorbed without breaking your environment.
  5. Measure the results. Tie each change to a concrete outcome—faster registration, cleaner data, reduced manual effort—so the portfolio stays accountable.

Ellucian Colleague is a comprehensive ERP platform designed exclusively for higher education institutions. It provides a unified system for managing student information, finance, human resources, and other core campus operations. Unlike generic ERP systems, Colleague is tailored for the unique workflows, compliance needs, and reporting requirements of colleges and universities. Its modular architecture enables institutions to configure processes around admissions, registration, degree audit, financial aid, and more—all within a secure, FERPA-compliant environment.

Key features include:

  • Student information management: Centralizes student records, registration, grades, and advising
  • Financial and HR management: Streamlines budgeting, payroll, and personnel processes
  • Self-service portals: Empowers students, faculty, and staff with personalized access to services
  • Robust reporting and analytics: Facilitates data-driven decision-making and compliance
  • Integration capabilities: Connects with other EdTech platforms, learning management systems, and third-party tools

Colleague is often the system of record for institutions running complex, multi-campus environments, supporting everything from admissions to graduation.

What sets Colleague apart is its ability to adapt to the evolving needs of higher education. Forefront Content:
What is Ellucian Colleague, and why does consulting matter?

Colleague is an enterprise resource planning (ERP) and student information system (SIS) built specifically for higher education, and institutions that run it, such as enterprise resource planning (ERP) system, note that the Ellucian software package includes Student, Financial, and Human Resources information systems. It ties together the offices that keep an institution moving — the registrar, the bursar, financial aid, HR, finance, and academic units — into a shared system of record. When it works well, a student's application, enrollment, billing, and transcript all flow through the same environment without staff rekeying data or reconciling conflicting reports.

The challenge is that Colleague is deep and highly configurable, and most institutions inherit a version of it that has been shaped by years of turnover, one-off customizations, and workarounds that made sense at the time but were never revisited. Business rules drift from published policy. Reports pull different numbers depending on who runs them. Integrations that once connected cleanly begin to break as surrounding systems change. None of this shows up as a single dramatic failure — it accumulates as friction, manual effort, and quiet risk.

Consulting matters because closing that gap requires two things at once: expertise in the platform itself and a genuine understanding of higher-education operations. Knowing which Colleague screen controls a fee assessment is useful; knowing why your financial aid office assesses that fee the way it does, and how that decision affects the student experience three steps downstream, is what actually produces durable improvements. Effective consulting connects the configuration to the outcome — fewer redundancies, lower operating cost, and a smoother path for students and staff.

‍

When should your institution bring in consulting support?

Most leaders don't wake up thinking they need outside help with their SIS. The need reveals itself through recurring symptoms. If several of the following sound familiar, it's usually time to bring in specialized support:

  • You're planning or recovering from an upgrade. Moving to a newer release, adopting cloud-hosted or SaaS deployment, or cleaning up a rushed migration all carry technical and process risk that dedicated experience can de-risk.
  • Institutional knowledge walked out the door. A retiring analyst or a departed director often takes years of undocumented configuration logic with them, leaving the team unsure why the system behaves the way it does.
  • Manual work keeps multiplying. Staff export data to spreadsheets, re-enter information between offices, or run overnight processes by hand — signs that the system isn't automating what it should.
  • Reporting can't be trusted. Leadership gets conflicting enrollment or financial numbers depending on the source, which stalls decisions and erodes confidence.
  • Integrations are fragile. Every new tool — a CRM, an LMS, a payment platform, a document imaging system — becomes a custom, brittle connection that breaks with each update.
  • An audit or compliance requirement is looming. New reporting mandates, security reviews, or data-privacy obligations expose gaps that need structured remediation.

There's also the strategic trigger: a new president, provost, or CIO who wants a clear-eyed assessment of what the current environment can and can't support. In each of these cases, the value of consulting isn't just fixing today's problem — it's building the internal capability and documentation so the same problem doesn't return.

‍

What services does this engagement include?

A strong engagement is scoped to the institution's actual need, not sold as a monolithic package. In practice, such work tends to span a handful of complementary service areas, and most institutions draw on more than one:

  • Assessment and roadmapping. A technology and business process assessment establishes where you stand today — what's configured, what's customized, where manual effort concentrates, and where risk lives — then translates that into a prioritized plan tied to budget and outcomes.
  • Optimization Services. Rather than replacing the platform, this work tunes it: streamlining workflows, retiring unnecessary customizations, aligning configuration with current policy, and eliminating the redundant steps that slow staff down. The goal is to get more value from the investment you've already made.
  • Integration Services. Consultants design and build reliable connections between Colleague and the surrounding ecosystem — CRM, LMS, payment, HR, and third-party point solutions — so data moves cleanly and stays consistent across systems.
  • Reporting and Analytics Services. This is about giving leaders a single, trustworthy version of the truth: well-defined data sources, accurate operational and compliance reporting, and dashboards that decision-makers can actually rely on.
  • Managed Services. For institutions short on internal staff, ongoing support keeps the environment healthy — handling routine administration, patching, monitoring, and issue resolution so the SIS stays stable without stretching the team thin.
  • Data governance and security alignment. Clarifying who owns which data, how it's defined, and how it's protected — with practices aligned to frameworks like FERPA, NIST, and ISO 27001 — turns compliance from a fire drill into a standing discipline.

The common thread is that each service produces something concrete: a documented roadmap, a working integration, a validated report, a governed data definition. The point isn't activity — it's measurable improvement your team can see and sustain.

‍

How consultants optimize and integrate your environment

Good outcomes come from a disciplined method, not heroics. While every institution is different, an effective engagement generally follows a recognizable sequence:

  1. Discover. Consultants document the current state — configuration, customizations, integrations, reports, and the business processes that sit on top of them. Critically, this includes interviewing the people who use the system daily, because the real workflow often differs from the one on paper.
  2. Diagnose and prioritize. Findings get sorted by impact and effort. A brittle integration that jeopardizes financial aid disbursement gets attention before a cosmetic reporting request. This is where Data Governance enters: agreeing on definitions, ownership, and quality standards so that everything built afterward rests on a trustworthy foundation.
  3. Design. Recommendations are translated into specific, buildable solutions — a redesigned workflow, a re-architected integration, a rationalized report catalog — each with a clear owner, timeline, and expected result.
  4. Implement. Changes are configured and tested in a controlled way, with rollback plans and validation against real institutional scenarios rather than generic test cases.
  5. Govern and transfer. The final step is often the most neglected and the most valuable: documenting what changed and why, establishing the governance and security routines that keep the environment healthy, and coaching internal staff so the institution isn't dependent on outside help forever.

Integration deserves special attention because it's where so much fragility originates. Interfaces enable information to be immediately shared across systems, including financial aid, registrar, and student enrollment, among others. Instead of building yet another one-off connection, seasoned consultants favor consistent, maintainable patterns — standard interfaces, monitored data flows, and clear documentation — so that when a surrounding system updates, the connection bends instead of breaking. That discipline, paired with strong IT Governance, is what separates an environment that quietly improves over time from one that degrades with every change. For deeper insight into integration challenges and solutions, see How easy is it to integrate Ellucian Colleague with other campus technologies like learning management systems?

The optimization mindset is equally important. It's tempting to treat every gap as a reason to buy new software, but a well-run assessment frequently reveals that the platform can already do what's needed — it simply hasn't been configured to. Portfolio rationalization often surfaces here too: identifying overlapping tools that can be consolidated to cut cost and complexity while improving the experience for students and staff alike.

‍

Choosing a consulting partner

The market is full of firms that know software. Far fewer bring people who have actually run the offices your solution will affect. That distinction should drive your selection. When evaluating a partner for this work, weigh the following:

  • Practitioner experience, not just product certification. Our consultants are former registrars, CIOs, and EdTech executives who have sat in your chair. That insider perspective means recommendations account for accreditation deadlines, financial aid rules, and the political realities of institutional change — not just technical feasibility.
  • The ability to bridge strategy and execution. Plenty of firms will hand you a strategy deck; fewer will stay to build it. Look for a partner that can both advise and do the work, so the roadmap doesn't stall the moment the engagement ends.
  • Flexible engagement models. Needs vary, so delivery should too. Project-based Advisory work suits a defined initiative with a fixed scope and timeline. On-demand support through Doctums Now is built for targeted questions and short bursts of expert help that reduce delays and errors. And when you need embedded, ongoing capacity, Endeavor provides fractional or full-time dedicated resources that flex with the institution's demands.
  • Senior, US-based delivery with clear deliverables. You want experienced people accountable to specific timelines, budgets, and outcomes — not a rotating cast of junior staff learning on your dime.
  • A serious governance and security posture. Because Colleague holds sensitive student and financial data, your partner's practices should align with FERPA, NIST, ISO 27001, and privacy regulations like CCPA and GDPR as a matter of course.

The right partner leaves you stronger than they found you. That means measurable results during the engagement — reduced manual work, trustworthy reporting, stable integrations — and a team that understands its own system well enough to maintain the gains. Deep specialization across the Ellucian ecosystem matters here as well: institutions rarely run Colleague in isolation, and a consultant who understands how the SIS interacts with the broader technology landscape will spot risks and opportunities a single-tool specialist would miss.

Ellucian Colleague can be one of the most valuable assets your institution operates — or a persistent source of friction and risk. The difference usually comes down to whether the platform is actively managed by people who understand both the technology and the mission it serves. If you're weighing an assessment, an optimization effort, or ongoing support, the smartest first step is a candid conversation about where your environment stands today and what "better" would actually look like. Name: Community College Funding Is Going Outcomes-Based Everywhere. The Data Behind It Usually Isn't Ready.
Forefront Content:
House Bill 8 rewrote the economics of Texas community college funding. Since September 2023, the state's 50 community college districts have been funded on outcomes instead of enrollment, with 95 percent of state appropriations flowing through a performance tier tied to credentials of value, high-demand occupations, transfer success, and dual credit completion, plus added weight for economically disadvantaged, academically disadvantaged, and adult learners over 25.

‍

It's a well-intentioned model, rewarding colleges for credentials that lead somewhere, transfers, and completions. But it has a dependency the funding formula rarely gets credit for: it only works if the underlying data is right.

‍

This is not just a Texas story

Texas is the most aggressive version of this shift, but not the only one. Oregon approved a new formula in 2023 that phases in through 2024-25, tying up to 10 percent of state funding to completion and success metrics for underserved students. North Carolina passed Propel NC in its 2025 legislative session, moving away from a pure enrollment-based model, with dollars starting this fiscal year. Michigan's latest budget added a performance component to community college funding tied to tuition restraint. California's Student Centered Funding Formula, which ties roughly 10 percent of funding to outcomes plus an equity supplemental, has continued to expand.

‍

Five states, five mechanics, one direction: funding is moving toward proof of outcome, away from proof of seat-time. It's a matter of when, not if.

‍

The catch nobody put in the press release

To earn performance funding, a college has to prove the outcome happened, prove which student achieved it, and prove whether that student qualifies for a weighted bonus. In Texas that means SSN-based student identifiers, clean differentiation between award levels, and the ability to flag whether a student is economically disadvantaged, academically disadvantaged, or an adult learner, no matter what program or department they came through. Other states are building toward the same requirement.

‍

That last piece is where a lot of institutions get caught. Many colleges never tracked disadvantaged status for continuing education students; those programs were built as auxiliary functions, run with lighter systems and less process discipline than the credit-bearing academic side. Under an outcomes-based model, they can trigger real money, but only if the data behind them holds up. In Texas, the Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board (THECB) has enforced short, strict windows for institutions to flag and correct data errors, warning that uncorrected mistakes lead directly to under-allocated funds. There is no grace period for bad data.

‍

The money is real, and now it's genuinely contested

Texas colleges have responded to HB 8 on the record. Laredo College turned nearly 80 students into peer advisers, multiplying its advising staff sevenfold; President Minita Ramirez told the Texas Tribune the law pushed the college to fix disjointed advising systems that had let students fall through the cracks. Grayson College built out electronics and automation training ahead of new semiconductor plants from Texas Instruments and GlobiTech; President Jeremy McMillen told the Tribune: “Without HB 8 in the background, it's very difficult to imagine that we've been able to do that.” Dallas College partnered with three area universities on a credit-transfer portal so students can see which courses will count toward a bachelor's degree. A direct response to HB 8's transfer-success incentive.

‍

What's happened since should get every college's attention. In July 2026, the Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board disclosed that colleges outperformed HB 8's projections so significantly the state can no longer afford the incentive structure as designed. THECB trimmed the bonus weights for high-need students, economically disadvantaged, academically disadvantaged, and adult learners, to stay within a roughly $1.2 billion budget cap. Nearly a dozen colleges now face funding drops of 15 percent or more despite meeting their performance goals. Paris Junior College's president wrote that his college grew enrollment 20 percent and is still facing a $1.4 million cut: “Successful colleges should not be penalized for exceeding expectations.”

‍

That's the real lesson three years in. This is a fixed, increasingly competitive pool, and the accuracy of your data determines whether you're protected or at risk when the state has to make the math work.

‍

A dinner conversation that stuck with me

On a recent site visit, a community college's continuing education leader described a tension we hear constantly: his division has been treated for years as the part of the institution nobody budgets for, running on older processes and thinner staffing than the credit side, and it's the part now projected to grow fastest, landing in the area least equipped to track, report, or defend that growth. Growth alone doesn't protect an institution when the state is trimming a capped incentive pool.

‍

Where the real risk sits

We're currently doing exactly this kind of foundational work with that college, focused on continuing education, dual enrollment, and corporate services, three areas that sit outside the academic core but squarely inside most outcomes-based scoring models. None of it works if the systems behind those programs were never built to produce clean, defensible data.

‍

The engagement isn't labeled as funding-formula compliance work, and it doesn't need to be. It's business process review to find where operations create downstream reporting gaps, system configuration to cut manual workarounds and bring continuing education and dual enrollment up to the same rigor as the credit side, a data governance framework that clarifies who owns which data, and training that makes the new workflows stick instead of reverting after six months.

‍

None of it shows up in a legislative summary. All of it determines whether a college captures the funding it has earned, and whether a growing continuing education operation can scale without the data falling apart underneath it.

‍

This is the pattern, not the exception

We see the same shape of problem across most of our higher education clients, regardless of state or funding model. SIS and ERP platforms accumulate a decade of workarounds. Reporting lives in tribal knowledge instead of governed processes. Non-credit and auxiliary programs get the least investment even as they generate a growing share of institutional value and funding.

‍

Legislation like HB 8, and its counterparts elsewhere, doesn't create this problem. It just puts a dollar figure on it and, increasingly, a ceiling. The colleges that adapt well won't be the ones with the flashiest dashboard; they'll be the ones that did the less exciting work first: cleaning up the process, configuring the system to match how the institution operates, and building governance so the data holds up under scrutiny.

‍

If your institution is staring down a funding model, an enrollment surge, an accreditation cycle, or a board that wants better reporting, and you're not confident the data would hold up, that's a conversation worth having before the next reporting deadline forces it. 

‍

Name: Your Staff Is Already Using AI. Does Your Institution Know How?
Short Description: Right now, on a campus somewhere, a financial aid counselor is asking ChatGPT to draft a response to an appeal. Down the hall, a registrar's office staffer is running a transfer credit question through Claude. Neither filed a ticket. Neither asked IT to vet the tool. This is Shadow AI, also known as BYOAI (Bring Your Own AI), and by most current measures, it's already the norm on college and university campuses, not the exception.
Forefront Content:
Right now, on a campus somewhere, a financial aid counselor is asking ChatGPT to draft a response to an appeal. Down the hall, a registrar's office staffer is running a transfer credit question through Claude. Neither filed a ticket. Neither asked IT to vet the tool. This is Shadow AI, also known as BYOAI (Bring Your Own AI), and by most current measures, it's already the norm on college and university campuses, not the exception.

‍

The scale of it is bigger than most leadership teams assume

More than half of higher ed staff, 56 percent, report using AI tools that their institution didn't provide for work-related tasks, according to EDUCAUSE's 2026 research on AI and work in higher education. A separate 2026 EDUCAUSE study found the number climbs even higher when the question is simply whether staff use AI at all: 94 percent of higher ed professionals reported using AI tools for work in the prior six months, while only 54 percent said they were aware of any institutional policy governing that use, per coverage of the EDUCAUSE findings. 

‍

The gap here isn't awareness of AI. Staff clearly know it exists and clearly find it useful. The gap is visibility: institutions don't have a consistent picture of which tools are being used, by whom, or with what data.

‍

Why banning it doesn't close that gap

The instinct to prohibit AI tools outright is understandable, and it's also the one response that consistently fails. Roundtable research from MIT's Center for Information Systems Research, conducted with more than 70 data and technology executives, lands on a simple reason: banning a tool doesn't stop staff from valuing what it does for them. It just removes the institution's ability to see it happening. The behavior doesn't disappear. It goes quiet.

Higher ed's own numbers back this up. Even though 77 percent of colleges and universities report having some level of AI strategy, only 30 percent consider AI and analytics preparedness a top institutional priority, and governance and compliance rank among the lowest priorities at just 27 percent, according to Campus Technology's analysis of the shadow AI threat. Strategy documents exist. Governance discipline mostly doesn't.

‍

It's bigger than any individual chatbot

The instinct is to think of Shadow AI as "did someone open ChatGPT." That framing misses most of the problem. AI is now built directly into the tools staff already open every day: Microsoft's suite prompts users to let Copilot redesign a slide or summarize a spreadsheet, and a Google search returns an AI-generated summary before a single link. None of that requires downloading anything or asking permission. The real question isn't whether staff are using a chatbot. It's whether the institution has any line of sight into how AI, in any form, touches its data and its decisions.

‍

Where the risk actually shows up

Shadow AI rarely looks dramatic. It looks like one department standardizing on the free tier of ChatGPT while the team next door works in Claude or Gemini, each producing output that's starting to sound noticeably the same, because nobody agreed on which tool to use or how. It looks like a staff member uploading a spreadsheet of student records to get a fast analysis back, which the tool genuinely does well, without stopping to ask a slower but more important question: where did that data just go, and does it include anything protected, personal, or confidential? The analysis is usually correct. The upload is the part nobody thought through.

‍

The mistake institutions keep making

"The institutions we talk with are rarely deciding whether to ban AI or embrace it. The real work is building a governance model that protects student data and keeps critical thinking central to the learning experience, while accepting that staff and students are already using these tools every day."

Dana DeLapi, Director of Marketing, Doctums

‍

Institutions tend to land on one of two extremes: shutting AI down entirely, or not addressing it at all. Neither holds up. The heavy-handed approach pushes use further out of view and gives an institution the illusion of control without the reality of it. Ignoring the issue leaves data governance, and academic integrity, to chance. 

What works sits in between: a governance model that accepts AI is already part of how work gets done, protects the data that moves through it, and still holds space for the critical thinking students and staff are there to build. That last part matters specifically in higher ed, in a way it wouldn't in most other industries. These are institutions built to teach people how to think, not just how to produce output faster.

‍

A practical path forward

None of this starts with a policy document nobody reads. It starts with an honest inventory: which tools are actually in use, on which teams, touching which systems. From there, institutions can build usage guidelines that distinguish between free and paid tiers, since the two handle data very differently and that distinction is often the first thing that gets lost. Staff training matters as much as the policy itself; a rule nobody understands gets worked around the same way a ban does. And a governance structure spanning data security, operational systems, and how AI use gets documented gives an institution something concrete to point to when a board, an auditor, or an accreditor asks how AI is being managed.

This isn't a one-time project. It's an operating discipline, and the institutions that treat it that way will still have a defensible answer a year from now.

‍

The human part doesn't go away

There's a broader shift underneath all of this: the institutions handling AI well aren't the ones removing people from the equation, they're the ones being deliberate about what AI should capture and what still needs a person's judgment. It's a distinction Doctums thinks about closely in how we build our own AI-enabled work, including through Doctums Extend.

AI tools can't replace the tacit judgment a consultant, or a faculty member, or a seasoned administrator brings to a decision. Shadow AI is what happens when that distinction gets lost by accident. Good governance is what happens when an institution draws it on purpose.

‍

Where to start

If your institution doesn't have a clear picture of where AI is already being used, and by whom, that's the starting point, not the policy itself.

Name: Higher Ed's Real IT Shortage Isn't People. It's What They Take With Them.
Short Description: Ask a CIO in higher ed when their IT staffing shortage started, and most will point to the last year or two.
Forefront Content:
Ask a CIO in higher ed when their IT staffing shortage started, and most will point to the last year or two. AI got introduced, everything got more complicated, and suddenly the team felt too small. But EDUCAUSE was writing about this same shortage back in 1998, describing the same gap between open IT positions and the qualified people to fill them. This isn't a new problem wearing an AI costume. It's an old problem that finally got loud enough to hear.

‍

IT staffing shortages in higher education are not a new problem

Colleges and universities have struggled to recruit and retain IT talent for decades. Long before AI entered the conversation, institutions were already competing for technical talent against employers who could pay more and move faster. What has changed is not the shortage itself. What has changed is the amount of work sitting on top of it.

AI added a new layer of responsibility to teams that were already stretched. EDUCAUSE's 2026 workforce research found that institutional change, including the push around AI, is largely being absorbed at the team level rather than through any real redesign of how work gets staffed. Most teams expect they'll need to support their institution's AI strategy, and most of those same teams say they feel only somewhat prepared to do it. The shortage did not get worse overnight. It just became a lot harder to work around quietly.

‍

The shortage has two parts, not one

Most conversations about IT staffing shortages focus on headcount: not enough people to do the work. That is real, but it is only half the picture.

"The technology in higher ed keeps advancing, and that's a good thing. But the people who've spent ten or fifteen years growing into these systems carry knowledge that never made it into a manual. When they retire or move on, that knowledge often goes with them, and it compounds the staffing shortage as much as an empty seat does."

— Moira Kirkland, Senior Vice President, Doctums

Someone who started in IT support and became the administrator who understands exactly why a process works the way it does at their institution, not just how the system is supposed to work in theory, is carrying more than a job title. When that person leaves, the shortage of people compounds a shortage of knowledge, and the two make each other worse.

‍

Why the instinct to hire doesn't solve it

When a team is maxed out, the reflex is to bring in new technology or a new hire and hope it closes the gap. In practice, that rarely works, because the problem usually isn't the technology.

"The pattern I see over and over is institutions trying to buy their way out of a broken process with a new system, a new integration, or a new dashboard, without ever mapping out what's actually happening today. Technology doesn't fix a process that's fundamentally misaligned, it just makes the dysfunction faster."

— Zach Richards, Higher Education Consultant, Doctums

Richards' approach starts before any tool gets selected: getting the functional and technical teams in the same room, mapping the process together, and agreeing on what should happen before deciding which system supports it.

"Alignment has to come before automation," he says. "Everyone wants the new tool, but if the people who live in the process every day and the people who build the system don't agree on what's happening, you're just automating the disagreement."

‍

What actually helps: augmentation and optimization together

The instinct to treat staffing as a hiring problem misses what institutions actually need. It isn't a choice between bringing in outside help or improving how things run internally. It's both, at the same time.

Getting a process to run smoother, while still leveraging the team already in place, usually starts with staff augmentation: bringing in outside support to help map where the technology stands today, where the institution wants it in five years, and what road gets it there. From that foundation, institutions can start hiring deliberately for the skills they'll actually need down the line, instead of hiring reactively for whatever broke most recently.

This is where a partner earns its place, and it's rarely just an extra set of hands.

‍

  1. Capacity. It's access to several skill sets at once, the kind of range one new hire wouldn't cover on their own.
  1. Specialized expertise. Someone on campus might know their core system inside and out, but the moment a new integration comes up, an admissions tool, a student portal, whatever's next, that calls for skills that don't exist internally yet and probably don't justify hiring someone full time just for that.
  1. Continuity. Cloud migration is accelerating across higher ed, and getting there is never instant. Students keep enrolling and classes keep running while the current system still has to be maintained the entire time the new one is being built. That's effectively two jobs happening in parallel, on a team sized for one.

It's this exact gap, capacity, expertise, and continuity all at once, that's part of why Doctums exists. We see it often enough in our own work with institutions that it shapes how we think about staffing conversations from the start.

‍

Where the knowledge goes when people move on

Staffing support solves part of the problem. The other part is making sure institutional knowledge doesn't walk out the door when someone does.

That is where documentation becomes part of the strategy, not an afterthought. Refining and recording how an institution actually runs its processes builds a kind of legacy that outlasts any one person's tenure. 

‍

What comes next

None of this starts with a new hire or a new system. It starts with stepping back to see which teams need to be aligned, and finding a partner who can help optimize across all of it, not just patch the most visible gap.

If your team is stretched thin and you're not sure whether the answer is more hands, better alignment, or both, that conversation is a good place to begin. And if you're wondering how this connects to the way institutions are also navigating AI on campus day to day, we wrote about that here.

Name: Higher education software implementation companies
Forefront Content:
Few investments shape an institution's future like the systems that run it: the student information system, the ERP, the CRM, the analytics stack that leadership relies on to make decisions. Yet the software itself rarely determines success or failure. What determines it is the implementation: the people, planning, and process discipline that turn a signed contract into working technology your registrar, faculty, and students actually trust. That's why choosing among higher education software implementation companies is one of the most consequential decisions a campus technology leader will make.

‍

What do higher education software implementation companies do?

At the simplest level, these firms take enterprise software from purchase to production. But the real work is far broader than installation. A capable implementation partner translates institutional goals into system configuration, migrates decades of student and financial data, integrates dozens of connected applications, trains staff, and stabilizes operations long after go-live. The best partners understand that a campus is not a corporation. Academic calendars, financial aid regulations, accreditation reporting, and shared governance all shape how a system must behave.

In practice, an implementation partner typically owns or advises on several distinct workstreams:

  • Discovery and requirements gathering that documents how your institution actually operates, not how a vendor assumes it does.
  • System configuration and design aligned to registrar rules, billing structures, and academic policy.
  • Data migration and validation from legacy platforms, with reconciliation you can defend during an audit.
  • Integration between the core system and the surrounding ecosystem of learning management, payment, credentialing, and reporting tools.
  • Testing across functional units, including the messy edge cases that break in production.
  • Training and adoption support so staff use the system instead of building workarounds.
  • Post-launch support and optimization to resolve issues and mature the deployment over time.

The distinction that matters most is between firms that resell and install software and firms that own outcomes. Doctums consultants are former registrars, CIOs, and higher ed technology executives who have run these offices, so the guidance you receive reflects operational reality, not a generic playbook.

‍

Why do higher education software implementations fail?

Understanding failure is the fastest path to choosing a partner who can prevent it. A study published in International Research in Education found that many institutions of higher education are not deriving the expected benefits from their ERP implementations, tracing the root causes to poor system integration and stakeholder requirements that were never fully considered. A more recent systematic review of 37 studies on ERP in higher education reached a complementary conclusion: the benefits are real, but achieving them depends on thorough planning. In other words, implementations rarely fail because the software is broken. They fail because of predictable human and organizational patterns.

The most common causes include underestimating data quality problems, treating adoption as an afterthought, letting scope expand without governance, and relying on staff who are already fully consumed by their day jobs. A registrar cannot rebuild the entire course catalog in a new system while simultaneously running registration for 20,000 students. When institutions try, timelines slip and quality suffers.

Three failure patterns deserve special attention:

1. The knowledge gap. Internal teams may know the institution deeply but have never configured the specific platform being deployed, while the vendor's technical team knows the platform but not your institution. Successful projects bridge that gap with people who understand both.

2. The decision vacuum. Implementations stall when no one is empowered to make configuration decisions quickly. Strong governance, with clear roles, escalation paths, and a steering structure, keeps momentum.

3. The stabilization cliff. Many projects celebrate go-live and then step back just as real users flood the system. The weeks after launch are when adoption is won or lost.

A partner worth hiring will name these risks in your first conversation and show you, concretely, how their methodology mitigates each one.

‍

What services should you expect from an implementation partner?

The strongest firms working with colleges and universities offer more than a single project team. They provide a portfolio of capabilities that map to the full lifecycle of a system: before, during, and long after deployment. When evaluating higher education software implementation providers, look for depth across the following:

  • Technology and business process assessments that examine whether your workflows should be replicated or redesigned before they're rebuilt in new software.
  • Integration services that connect the core platform to your broader digital environment so data flows cleanly instead of being rekeyed.
  • Reporting and analytics enablement so leadership gets trustworthy dashboards from day one, not months later.
  • Data governance frameworks that define ownership, quality standards, and stewardship across departments.
  • Training and adoption enablement designed for academic culture, where success depends on faculty and staff buy-in.
  • Managed and optimization services that continue tuning the system as regulations, enrollment models, and institutional priorities evolve.

Delivery flexibility matters as much as service breadth. Some institutions need a defined, project-based engagement with fixed timelines and deliverables. Others need to fill a specific gap fast, such as a Banner functional expert for six weeks or a data migration specialist to unblock a stalled workstream. Still others need planned capacity that stays for a year. Doctums structures this as project-based advisory work, targeted expert support, and ongoing capacity through Doctums Extend, its skills-based managed services model, so the engagement model fits the problem instead of the reverse.

‍

How do you choose the right implementation company for your institution?

Selection should be a structured evaluation, not a reaction to the loudest sales pitch. The goal is to find a partner whose expertise, delivery model, and cultural fit match your specific platform and institutional context.

Start by matching specialization to your stack. A firm with deep experience in your particular ecosystem will spot risks a generalist misses. Institutions running Ellucian platforms, for example, need consultants fluent in the real behavior of Banner or Colleague, including how configuration choices ripple through registration, billing, and financial aid. Deep specialization in these ecosystems, along with Anthology Student environments, separates true experts from firms learning on your budget.

Then evaluate along these dimensions:

  • Practitioner credibility. Have the consultants actually held roles like the ones they're advising? Insider perspective shortens discovery and prevents costly missteps.
  • Seniority. Understand who will actually do the work. Senior consultants delivering the engagement themselves is very different from a senior name on the proposal and junior staff on the project.
  • Defined scope and accountability. Look for tailored delivery with specific timelines, budgets, and deliverables, not open-ended time-and-materials arrangements.
  • Governance and security posture. Confirm alignment with frameworks such as NIST and ISO 27001, plus compliance with FERPA and privacy regulations like CCPA and GDPR. Student data demands it.
  • Measurable outcomes. Ask how the firm defines and reports success: reduced redundancies, lower operating cost, faster processing, improved student experience.
  • Knowledge transfer. The best partners leave your team stronger, not more dependent. Confirm that documentation and enablement are built into the engagement.

Beware two extremes. The largest global integrators can bring scale but often assign teams unfamiliar with higher education's regulatory and cultural nuance. The smallest local shops may know your campus but lack platform depth. The sweet spot for many institutions is a specialized firm that combines both, operational insight and technical mastery, while bridging the gap between strategy and execution.

‍

What questions should you ask before signing a contract?

The proposal stage is where you separate marketing from method. Great answers to hard questions are the strongest predictor of a great implementation. Before you sign, put these on the table:

1. Who, specifically, will be on my team, and what have they implemented before? Ask for names, roles, and comparable projects, ideally at institutions similar to yours in size and mission.

2. How do you handle data migration and validation? Data is where projects quietly go wrong. You want a rigorous, documented approach with reconciliation checkpoints.

3. What does your training and adoption approach look like? If the answer is "we'll run a few sessions before go-live," keep looking. For deeper context on this critical phase, see how to increase adoption of our student system

4. How do you govern scope and decisions? Understand how change requests, escalations, and steering decisions are managed so the project doesn't drift.

5. What happens after go-live? Clarify the stabilization period, support model, and the point at which you can shift into optimization and ongoing improvement.

6. How do you protect our data and stay compliant? Expect specific references to security frameworks and privacy regulations, not vague reassurances.

7. How will we measure success together? Insist on defined outcomes and a reporting cadence agreed before work begins.

Document the answers. During delivery, they become the standard you hold your partner to.

‍

What does a successful higher education software implementation look like?

A successful implementation is quiet. Registration runs. Bills post accurately. Financial aid disburses on time. Leadership opens a dashboard and trusts the number. Staff use the system as designed rather than maintaining shadow spreadsheets, and the institution can point to concrete gains: hours reclaimed, redundant tools retired, costs optimized, and a measurably better experience for students.

Getting there follows a recognizable arc:

1. Align on outcomes before configuration begins, so every decision serves a defined goal.

2. Assess and, where warranted, redesign processes rather than automating inefficiency.

3. Configure, migrate, and integrate with disciplined testing at each stage.

4. Prepare people through training and adoption support that treats success as a first-class objective.

5. Go live with a stabilization plan and hands-on support through the first high-volume cycles.

Name: Are there any hidden costs or contractual terms we should look out for before renewing the ERP contract?
Forefront Content:
Renewing an ERP contract can feel like a formality, until you read the fine print. For many institutions, the price on the renewal quote is only part of the story, and the clauses deeper in the agreement can shape your budget and flexibility for years. Before you sign, it's worth pausing to ask a hard question: Are there any hidden costs or contractual terms we should look out for before renewing the ERP contract? More often than not, the answer is yes, and the earlier you find them, the more leverage you keep.

The true cost of renewal isn't on the first page

Renewal quotes tend to highlight your base license or subscription and little else. The real number is your total cost of ownership over the full term, which folds in support tiers, professional services, integrations, and the incremental fees that accumulate as your institution grows. Renewal deadlines create urgency, and urgency rarely produces careful reading. That's precisely when hidden costs slip through, not because they're concealed, but because no one has time to model them against three or five years of actual usage.

Hidden costs to uncover before you sign

The most expensive surprises are the ones that scale with your enrollment, your modules, or your data. As you evaluate the agreement, look specifically for:

  • Annual escalation clauses that raise your fees each year and compound over the contract term, sometimes faster than inflation.
  • Enrollment- or user-based pricing that increases as headcount grows, even when your actual system usage stays flat.
  • Module bundling, where features you rely on are packaged with ones you don't, and can't be unbundled at renewal.
  • Integration and API fees for connecting your CRM, LMS, or reporting tools, often billed per connector or per transaction volume.
  • Support tier changes that adjust your response times unless you pay to maintain your current level of service.
  • Cloud migration and hosting charges triggered when an on-premise product reaches end of life and a SaaS edition becomes the path forward.
  • Data extraction or egress fees charged if you ever need to export your records or leave the platform.

Any one of these can turn a "flat" renewal into a materially larger commitment. Modeling them against your real transaction data, not general assumptions, is where former registrars and CIOs tend to catch the discrepancies that a procurement checklist misses.

Contractual terms that quietly limit your options

Cost isn't the only thing worth scrutinizing. The terms that govern how and when you can change course often matter more than the price itself. Watch closely for the following:

  1. Auto-renewal and notice windows. Many agreements renew automatically unless you give notice well in advance, often several months before the term ends. Miss that window and you're committed to another full term at the stated rate.
  2. Termination for convenience. Confirm whether you can exit early, and at what penalty. One-sided termination rights leave your institution carrying the risk.
  3. Price caps. Without a negotiated ceiling on annual increases, you're accepting open-ended cost growth.
  4. Data ownership and portability. Verify in writing that your institutional data is yours, exportable in a usable format, without punitive fees.
  5. Audit and true-up rights. Some contracts allow usage audits and retroactive billing for overages, so make sure the terms are reasonable and reciprocal.
  6. SLA definitions. Uptime guarantees mean little without defined remedies when they're missed.

If you find yourself asking again whether there are hidden costs or restrictive contractual terms before renewal, treat that instinct as a signal to slow the process down rather than accelerate it.

How to prepare for a stronger renewal negotiation

The institutions that renew well start months early and negotiate from evidence. A practical sequence looks like this: first, inventory which modules and licenses you actually use versus what you pay for. Second, pull your real usage and enrollment data to model total cost across the full renewal term. Third, benchmark your pricing against comparable institutions running the same systems. Fourth, define your must-haves, such as price caps, exit rights, and data portability, before the renewal conversation begins. Finally, negotiate the terms, not just the number, since a favorable clause often outlasts a one-time discount.

Name: Are there any risks or challenges associated with enabling more integrations and automation within our existing SIS platform?
Forefront Content:
Enabling more integrations and automation across your student information system promises exactly what most institutions want: fewer manual handoffs, faster processes, cleaner data, and a better experience for students and staff. But those gains rarely come for free. Every new connection point and automated workflow adds a layer of complexity that can quietly undermine the very outcomes you're chasing. So are there any risks or challenges associated with enabling more integrations and automation within our existing SIS platform? Absolutely, and understanding them early is what separates a smooth rollout from an expensive cleanup.

Where the biggest risks tend to hide

Most integration failures don't announce themselves. They show up weeks later as a duplicate financial aid record, a transcript that won't post, or an enrollment count that no two departments agree on. The more systems you connect, such as CRM, LMS, payment platforms, degree audit, and identity providers, the more places a small error can spread before anyone notices. The core challenges typically fall into a few buckets:

  • Data integrity: mismatched field mappings, sync timing conflicts, and duplicate records that erode trust in your reporting.
  • Security risk: each new API or credential expands your attack surface and your compliance obligations.
  • Operational fragility: automations that work well until an upstream system changes a data format overnight.
  • Change fatigue: staff who no longer understand which system is the source of truth.

Data integrity and governance challenges

Automation only accelerates what you feed it. If the underlying data is inconsistent, you're now spreading bad information faster and to more places. That's why strong Data Governance has to precede, not follow, any expansion of automated workflows. You need clear ownership of each data domain, agreed-upon definitions for shared fields, and a documented system of record so that a "student status" change in one platform doesn't silently contradict another. Institutions that skip this step often discover that their new automations are technically flawless yet functionally untrustworthy, forcing staff back into the manual reconciliation those tools were supposed to eliminate.

‍

Security and compliance risk

Every integration is a doorway, and doorways need locks. When you enable more connections into an SIS holding financial, health, and academic records, you inherit real obligations under FERPA, and often CCPA or GDPR depending on your population. Poorly scoped API permissions, hard-coded credentials, and unmonitored data flows are among the most common sources of risk when institutions rush to automate. Sound practice means aligning integration design with recognized frameworks like NIST and ISO 27001, applying least-privilege access, encrypting data in transit and at rest, and logging every automated transaction so you can prove who touched what and when. Cybersecurity isn't a bolt-on here. It's a design constraint that should shape which integrations you enable at all.

‍

Operational and change management challenges

The technical risks that come with expanding integrations and automation in your SIS are often easier to solve than the human ones. Automated workflows change how people do their jobs, sometimes removing steps staff have relied on for years to catch errors. Without deliberate Change Management, you get shadow processes, workarounds, and quiet distrust of the new system. There's also the ongoing maintenance burden: automations are not "set and forget." Platform updates, patch cycles, and evolving business rules mean that a workflow which runs perfectly today can break silently tomorrow. Someone has to own monitoring, testing, and remediation, or the efficiency you gained slowly leaks back out.

‍

How to enable integrations and automation safely

The good news is that none of these challenges of automating and integrating your student information system are reasons to avoid the work. They're reasons to sequence it well. A disciplined approach usually looks like this:

  1. Assess before you connect. Map your current data flows, sources of truth, and process pain points so you automate the right things, not just the easy ones.
  2. Govern first. Establish data ownership, field definitions, and security standards before turning on new connections.
  3. Pilot narrowly. Prove one high-value integration end to end, with monitoring and rollback plans, before scaling.
  4. Build for maintenance. Document every workflow and assign ongoing ownership through Integration Services or Managed Services support so nothing runs unwatched.
  5. Bring people along. Train staff on the new source of truth and give them a clear escalation path when something looks wrong.

Name: What are the current trends in educational technology?
Forefront Content:
Educational technology is moving faster than most campus roadmaps can keep pace with. Between AI-driven tutoring, cloud-based student information systems, and analytics platforms that flag at-risk students before they disappear, the tools available to colleges have changed dramatically in just a few years. For leaders balancing tight budgets against rising student expectations, knowing which shifts genuinely matter is half the battle. This guide breaks down the developments worth your attention and, just as importantly, how to act on them.

Why higher ed technology trends matter more than ever

Technology decisions in higher education are no longer confined to the IT department. When a learning platform underperforms or a system integration breaks, the ripple effects hit enrollment, retention, financial aid, and the day-to-day experience of every student and faculty member. That's why understanding what are the current trends in educational technology has become a strategic concern for presidents, provosts, and CFOs, not just CIOs. Falling behind isn't merely a missed convenience; it can mean higher operating costs, frustrated staff working around clunky tools, and students who choose other institutions offering a smoother digital experience.

The biggest trends shaping education technology today

The landscape is broad, but a handful of movements are reshaping how institutions operate and serve learners. The 2026 EDUCAUSE Top 10, ranked through a survey of EDUCAUSE members, puts collaborative cybersecurity in the number one spot, followed by the human edge of AI, with data analytics for operational and financial insights and a data-centric institutional culture close behind. The most consequential trends in education technology right now include:

  • Artificial intelligence and automation: from AI tutoring and chatbots that handle routine student inquiries to predictive models that identify students at risk of stopping out, giving advisors time to intervene.
  • Cloud migration and modernization: legacy on-premise systems are giving way to cloud-hosted platforms that reduce infrastructure overhead and enable faster updates.
  • Data analytics and reporting: leaders increasingly want real-time dashboards, not quarterly reports, so they can act on enrollment and performance signals as they emerge.
  • System integration and interoperability: as campuses adopt more specialized tools, connecting the SIS, LMS, CRM, and finance systems into one coherent flow has become essential.
  • Cybersecurity and data governance: with FERPA obligations and rising ransomware threats, protecting student data now sits at the center of every technology conversation.
  • Personalized and flexible learning: hybrid course models, adaptive content, and mobile-first design reflect students who expect the same responsiveness they get from consumer apps.

Notice how many of these overlap. AI is only as good as the data feeding it, and clean data depends on well-integrated systems and disciplined governance. The trends aren't separate initiatives so much as interlocking pieces of a modern digital campus.

How institutions are turning trends into outcomes

Recognizing a trend is easy; operationalizing it is where most projects stall. The institutions making real progress tend to follow a consistent sequence:

  1. Assess honestly. Start with a clear-eyed technology and business process assessment: what's working, what's redundant, and where costs are hiding.
  2. Prioritize by impact. Rank opportunities by their effect on students and the bottom line, not by which demo was flashiest.
  3. Fix the foundation first. Modernizing a student information system such as Banner or Colleague, or tightening integrations, often unlocks more value than a new front-end tool.
  4. Govern the data. Establish ownership, quality standards, and security controls so analytics and AI have something trustworthy to work with.
  5. Measure and iterate. Track defined outcomes, such as reduced processing time, improved retention, and lower licensing spend, and adjust.

What to weigh before you invest

Chasing every trend is a fast way to overspend and under-deliver. Before committing budget, thoughtful leaders ask a few grounding questions: Does this solve a documented problem or just add capability? Can our team support it after go-live? How does it connect to systems we already run? And does the security and compliance posture hold up under FERPA and modern threat expectations?

Name: What are the different types of SIS systems?
Forefront Content:
If you've ever tried to compare student information systems, you know the landscape can feel crowded and confusing. These platforms sit at the center of campus life, spanning admissions, registration, financial aid, billing, advising, and graduation, yet no two are architected the same way. Understanding the categories makes the buying decision far clearer, whether you're modernizing a legacy environment or evaluating your first enterprise platform. Here's a practical breakdown.

‍

What a student information system does

Before sorting the categories, it helps to anchor on function. A student information system (SIS) is the system of record for the student lifecycle. It manages enrollment, course catalogs, grades, transcripts, degree audits, financial aid packaging, and student accounts. When people ask What are the different types of SIS systems?, they're usually trying to figure out which deployment model, market fit, and vendor ecosystem match their institution's size, budget, and technical capacity. Those three lenses (how it's hosted, who it serves, and whose ecosystem it belongs to) are the clearest way to organize the field.

‍

The main types of SIS systems by deployment

The first way to distinguish platforms is by where and how they run. This is often the biggest driver of cost, staffing, and long-term flexibility.

  • On-premise SIS: Software installed and maintained on the institution's own servers. It offers maximum control and deep customization, but it demands significant IT staff, hardware, and ongoing patching. Many established universities still run mature on-premise deployments.
  • Cloud-based (SaaS) SIS: Hosted and maintained by the vendor and delivered over the web. These reduce infrastructure overhead, push automatic updates, and scale more easily, which makes them an increasingly common choice for institutions modernizing aging systems.
  • Hybrid SIS: A blend that keeps some functions on-premise while moving others, like reporting, analytics, or the constituent-facing portal, to the cloud. This is often a transitional model for institutions migrating in phases.

The deployment question rarely has a universal answer. It depends on how much control you need, how lean your IT team is, and how much you value predictable, vendor-managed maintenance.

‍

SIS platforms by institution and market

Not every platform is built for every campus. The category you consider should reflect the type of institution you run.

  1. K-12 systems focus on attendance, gradebooks, parent communication, and state reporting.
  2. Higher education systems handle far more complexity: multi-term registration, financial aid, degree audits, bursar operations, and integrations with the LMS, CRM, and payment systems.
  3. Vertical or specialty systems serve niche needs, such as continuing education, trade and career schools, or international programs, where standard enterprise suites may be more than an institution requires.

For colleges and universities, this distinction matters because a purpose-built higher ed platform will speak the language of registrars, financial aid officers, and provosts far better than a general-purpose or downmarket tool.

‍

Major SIS vendors and ecosystems

Once you know your deployment model and market, the practical question becomes which vendor ecosystem fits. According to ListEdTech's January 2025 market data, Ellucian Banner leads the North American higher ed SIS market with 24 percent share, followed by Ellucian Colleague, Jenzabar, and Oracle PeopleSoft Campus Solutions. Since then, Ellucian has also completed its acquisition of Anthology's SIS and ERP business, bringing Anthology Student into the same ecosystem. Workday Student continues to gain ground, Populi serves a growing number of smaller institutions, and newer cloud-native platforms such as Student First are built specifically for non-traditional institutions. The differences aren't just cosmetic. Each ecosystem carries distinct data models, reporting tools, and customization limits, which means the "right" choice depends heavily on your existing infrastructure and staff expertise. This is where insider familiarity pays off: our consultants are former registrars, CIOs, and higher ed technology leaders who have operated these systems from the inside, so decisions are grounded in how the platforms actually behave in production, not just in a sales demo.

‍

How to choose the right SIS type

Choosing among the different kinds of SIS is less about finding the "best" system and more about matching the right category to your institution's reality. Weigh deployment against your IT capacity, market fit against your student population, and ecosystem against the tools you already run. Factor in migration effort, integration requirements, total cost of ownership, and change management for the people who use the system daily. The categories of student information systems only get you to the shortlist; disciplined evaluation gets you to the right decision.
