Name: What strategies can institutions use to reduce the financial impact of software sprawl without disrupting essential services?
Forefront Content:
Higher education runs on software: student information systems, learning platforms, CRMs, analytics tools, and a long tail of departmental subscriptions nobody fully tracks. Over time that accumulation becomes software sprawl: overlapping licenses, shadow IT driven by departmental autonomy, and renewal invoices that quietly erode already-tight budgets. The instinct to cut spending is correct, but removing tools carelessly can break enrollment, financial aid, or advising workflows students depend on. So the real question is what strategies can institutions use to reduce the financial impact of software sprawl without disrupting essential services?

Why software sprawl costs more than the license fees

The line-item cost of a subscription is only the visible tip of the problem. Every redundant platform carries integration maintenance, support overhead, training time, and an expanded security surface that invites risk. When three departments buy three different survey tools, or two systems duplicate the same reporting function, the institution pays repeatedly for capability it already owns. Sprawl also fragments data, forcing staff to reconcile conflicting records across systems that were never designed to talk to each other. That's why EDUCAUSE placed measured approaches to new technologies, including clear cost, ROI, and legacy systems assessments, among its 2026 Top 10 IT issues. Trimming that waste protects both the budget and the student experience, provided you know exactly what you have before you cut.

How can institutions audit their software portfolio without slowing operations?

You cannot rationalize what you have not measured. A structured Technology and Business Process Assessment inventories every application, its owner, its true annual cost, and the workflows that depend on it, so consolidation decisions rest on evidence rather than guesswork. A practical sequence looks like this:

  1. Build a complete inventory. Capture licensed systems, departmental subscriptions, and shadow IT surfaced through expense and network data.
  2. Map dependencies. Document which tools feed essential services, such as registration, aid disbursement, and transcripts, so nothing critical is touched by accident.
  3. Score overlap and utilization. Flag duplicate functionality and low-adoption licenses that generate cost without value.
  4. Model total cost of ownership. Include integration, support, and renewal terms, not just the sticker price.
  5. Prioritize by risk and savings. Rank candidates for consolidation, renegotiation, or retirement.

Portfolio Rationalization turns that inventory into a defensible roadmap: keep what performs, consolidate what overlaps, and sunset what no longer earns its place. Because former registrars, CIOs, and higher ed technology leaders have run these systems from the inside, the assessment reflects how the tools are actually used on campus, not how a datasheet describes them. For institutions looking to understand their current technology landscape more deeply, see how to audit our higher education tech stack.

What strategies protect essential services during consolidation?

The difference between smart savings and operational disruption is sequencing. Cutting cost is easy; cutting cost while the term-start deadline holds firm is the discipline. A few principles keep essential systems running throughout the effort:

  • Phase retirements around the academic calendar so nothing changes during registration, census, or aid processing peaks.
  • Preserve data and integrations first. Before decommissioning a tool, confirm its data has a validated home and its downstream connections are rerouted. Strong Integration Services prevent the broken handoffs that trigger service outages.
  • Govern the decisions. Clear IT Governance defines who approves a retirement, who owns the risk, and how exceptions are handled, which stops sprawl from quietly regrowing.
  • Communicate and train. Structured Change Management brings faculty and staff along, so consolidation improves adoption instead of breeding new shadow workarounds.

Institutions running Ellucian environments like Banner especially benefit from consolidating around a well-configured core rather than adding redundant point solutions, since each unnecessary add-on multiplies integration and support cost. The goal is to reduce spending while every mission-critical process keeps functioning exactly as students and staff expect.

Turning one-time savings into lasting financial discipline

A single cleanup produces headline savings; without governance, sprawl simply returns within a couple of budget cycles. The institutions that stay lean treat rationalization as an ongoing practice. Optimization Services keep configurations tuned and licenses right-sized as needs evolve, while an intake process requires new software requests to justify cost, overlap, and integration burden before purchase. For teams without the internal bandwidth to sustain this, ongoing support through a managed services model like Doctums Extend can carry the discipline forward: maintaining the roadmap, monitoring renewals, and catching duplication before it lands on an invoice. That combination is how you keep reducing the drag of software sprawl on the budget without ever putting essential services at risk. Handled this way, cost control becomes a repeatable capability rather than a one-time project, and the savings compound year over year instead of eroding.

Name: How do we know if our student system is delivering ROI
Forefront Content:
Your student information system is likely one of the largest and longest-lived technology investments on campus, yet few institutions can say with confidence that it's earning its keep. Ask a room of administrators how do we know if our student system is delivering ROI, and you'll hear everything from annual license costs to gut feelings about overworked registrar staff. The question is gaining urgency: EDUCAUSE named measured approaches to new technologies, grounded in clear cost, ROI, and legacy systems assessments, one of its 2026 Top 10 IT issues. The truth is that return on a student system is measurable, but only when you look past the sticker price to the outcomes it actually produces. Here's how to build that clarity.

‍

What ROI actually means for a student information system

Return on investment for a student system isn't simply cost recovery against your subscription or maintenance fees. It's the total value the platform creates against the total cost of owning and operating it, and much of that value hides in places finance dashboards never capture. When you evaluate whether the system is delivering, weigh these dimensions together:

  • Operational efficiency: hours reclaimed from manual registration, transcript, financial aid, and reconciliation work.
  • Student experience: faster enrollment, fewer errors, self-service that actually works.
  • Data quality and trust: a single, accurate record leadership can plan and report against.
  • Avoided costs: retired point solutions, reduced overtime, fewer compliance risks.
  • Strategic agility: how quickly the platform can support new programs, modalities, or policies.

A system can look "fully paid for" on a spreadsheet while quietly draining thousands of staff hours, so real ROI lives in the gap between what you spend and the outcomes above.

‍

The signals that reveal whether your SIS is paying off

You rarely need a formal study to sense trouble. The strongest early indicators of weak return show up in daily behavior. Watch for staff maintaining spreadsheets that shadow the official record, chronic duplicate data entry between offices, month-end reporting that takes days instead of minutes, and modules you paid for but never fully turned on. When admissions, registrar, and financial aid teams each keep their own "real" version of the truth, the system isn't unifying the institution. It's being worked around. Healthy signals look like the opposite: clean handoffs between offices, reports leadership trusts on the first pass, and students completing key tasks without picking up the phone. If most of your evidence points to workarounds, you already have a partial answer to whether your student system is delivering ROI, and a clear place to start measuring.

‍

How to measure student system ROI step by step

Turning impressions into a defensible number is a structured exercise, not a guess. A disciplined approach follows a repeatable sequence:

  1. Establish a baseline. Document how core processes, such as registration, awarding aid, producing transcripts, and closing terms, perform today in time, error rates, and cost.
  2. Total the true cost of ownership. Combine licensing, hosting, integrations, internal labor, and the price of workarounds and shadow systems.
  3. Quantify realized value. Translate reclaimed hours, avoided tools, and reduced errors into dollars, then layer in experience gains that drive retention.
  4. Benchmark against potential. Compare current use to what your platform is capable of; unused functionality is unrealized ROI.
  5. Model the gap. The distance between today's baseline and achievable performance is your improvement opportunity, and your business case.

This is exactly the work our Technology and Business Process Assessments are built to do: map how your people, processes, and platform actually interact, then quantify where value is leaking. Because our consultants are former registrars and CIOs, the measurement reflects how the work really happens, not a generic checklist.

‍

Why student systems quietly underperform

Most systems don't fail loudly; they drift. Over years of turnover, patches, and one-off customizations, configuration decisions accumulate until the platform no longer matches how the institution operates. Integrations built for a prior era pass stale or partial data, so offices stop trusting the system and rebuild processes by hand. Modules purchased in a bundle go unconfigured because no one had time to implement them. Weak data and IT governance let each department bend the system to local needs, fragmenting the single record. None of these are platform defects. They're accumulated debt. ‍

From assessment to measurable gains

Knowing whether your student system is delivering ROI is only useful if it drives change. Once the assessment reveals the gap, the fix is usually a prioritized roadmap: reconfigure what's misaligned, retire redundant tools, tighten integrations, and stand up Reporting and Analytics Services so leadership can watch the metrics improve quarter over quarter. That's the difference between a system you tolerate and one that earns its investment. Name: How to audit our higher education tech stack
Forefront Content:
Most colleges and universities don't buy technology all at once; they accumulate it. A student information system here, a new CRM there, a dozen departmental point solutions purchased over a decade, each with its own contract, login, and data silo. Left unexamined, that sprawl quietly drains budgets, fragments student data, and widens security gaps. Understanding how to audit our higher education tech stack is the first step toward reclaiming control, cutting redundancy, and building a portfolio that actually serves your mission.

‍

Why audit your higher education technology stack?

An audit answers a question most institutions can't confidently answer: what do we actually own, and is it earning its keep? Software costs rarely shrink on their own. Overlapping licenses, underused platforms, and orphaned subscriptions add up fast, often to a meaningful share of the technology budget. It's no coincidence that EDUCAUSE named measured approaches to new technologies, built on clear cost, ROI, and legacy systems assessments, one of its 2026 Top 10 IT issues. Beyond cost, a fragmented stack creates friction for students who bounce between disconnected systems and for staff who rekey the same data across tools. A disciplined review of your campus technology stack surfaces those inefficiencies and gives leadership the evidence to act. The goal isn't a spreadsheet of applications. It's a clear line of sight from every system to the outcomes it supports.

‍

What should a technology stack audit include?

A thorough evaluation of your technology portfolio goes well beyond listing software. At minimum, it should capture:

  • Application inventory: every system in use, including shadow IT purchased outside central oversight.
  • Contracts and spend: renewal dates, license counts, and the true annual cost per platform.
  • Integrations and data flows: how systems connect, where data moves, and where it breaks.
  • Usage and adoption: who actually uses each tool, and how often.
  • Security and compliance posture: alignment with FERPA and frameworks like NIST and ISO 27001.
  • Ownership and governance: who is accountable for each system and the decisions around it.

Together, these dimensions turn a vague sense of "too many tools" into a defensible, prioritized picture.

‍

How to audit your higher education tech stack step by step

A structured process keeps the audit from stalling. A practical sequence looks like this:

  1. Define scope and goals. Decide whether you're reviewing the full enterprise or a single domain, such as your Ellucian Banner or Colleague environment.
  2. Build the inventory. Pull data from procurement, IT, and department heads to catalog every application and contract.
  3. Map integrations and data. Document how systems talk to one another and where manual workarounds fill the gaps.
  4. Assess each system. Score tools on cost, adoption, risk, and strategic fit.
  5. Identify redundancies and risks. Flag overlapping capabilities, security risks, and expiring contracts.
  6. Prioritize and recommend. Rank opportunities by impact and effort, then map them to a realistic roadmap.

Because our consultants are former registrars, CIOs, and technology leaders, they know where these findings tend to hide, and how to weigh them against real institutional constraints.

‍

What problems does an audit typically uncover?

Nearly every audit turns up the same culprits. Redundant platforms, meaning multiple tools doing the same job, top the list, usually because departments purchased independently without a shared intake process. Integration debt is close behind: brittle, manual connections that break during upgrades and force staff into duplicate data entry. Others include underused licenses paid for but never adopted, inconsistent data definitions that undermine reporting, and gaps where sensitive student records lack proper controls. Portfolio Rationalization, systematically consolidating and retiring overlapping systems, is often the single highest-return outcome of the entire exercise.

‍

How do you turn audit findings into action?

Findings only matter if they drive change. The strongest audits end with a sequenced roadmap that ties each recommendation to a measurable outcome: reduced spend, faster processes, tighter security, or a smoother student experience. That usually means strengthening IT Governance so future purchases follow a clear decision process, tackling quick wins first to build momentum, and pairing technical fixes with the change management needed to make new workflows stick. Institutions often bridge the gap between strategy and execution with ongoing support that carries recommendations through to delivery rather than leaving them in a report. Name: How to increase adoption of our student system
Forefront Content:
Rolling out a new or upgraded student information system is a massive investment, but the technology only pays off when your registrars, advisors, faculty, and students actually use it. Too often, institutions go live only to watch staff quietly revert to spreadsheets, shadow processes, and workarounds. If you're wondering how to increase adoption of our student system, the answer rarely lies in the software itself; it lies in the people, incentives, and support structures around it. Here's a practitioner's view of what actually moves the needle.

‍

Why does adoption of a student system stall?

Most adoption problems trace back to a launch that treated go-live as the finish line instead of the starting point. The platform gets configured, a few training sessions happen, and then the project team disbands, leaving end users to fend for themselves the moment real registration or financial aid pressure hits. Adoption also stalls when the system solves an IT problem but ignores day-to-day workflow. A registrar who now needs seven clicks to do what used to take two will find a faster path outside the system every time. Common culprits include:

  • Training built around features, not the tasks users perform daily
  • No visible executive sponsorship signaling that the new system is mandatory
  • Legacy processes left running in parallel, giving staff an easy exit
  • Poor data quality that erodes trust in what the system reports

‍

What drives low user adoption?

Low adoption is almost always a trust and relevance problem before it's a technology problem. When users don't believe the data is accurate, or don't see how the platform makes their week easier, they disengage. The most predictable driver is a gap between how the system was configured and how the institution actually operates: decisions made in a conference room that never accounted for the messy realities of advising holds, transfer credit, or term-based billing. Change fatigue matters too. Campuses that have absorbed several disruptive rollouts in a few years meet each new one with understandable skepticism. Strong Change Management closes that gap by involving frontline staff in design decisions early, so the people who live in the system feel ownership rather than imposition. As former registrars and CIOs, we've seen that the institutions with the highest adoption are the ones that treated culture as seriously as configuration.

‍

How to increase adoption of your student system

Boosting engagement is a deliberate program, not a one-time event. A proven sequence looks like this:

  1. Map the real workflows. Document how each office actually completes core tasks, then configure or reconfigure the system to match, or consciously improve, those steps rather than forcing users into an awkward default.
  2. Recruit champions in every department. Identify respected power users who can answer peer questions, model best practices, and surface friction before it spreads.
  3. Retire the workarounds. Decommission legacy screens, shadow spreadsheets, and parallel processes so the new system becomes the path of least resistance.
  4. Deliver role-based, task-based training. Teach an advisor how to place a hold, not how to navigate a menu tree. Short, scenario-driven sessions outperform daylong feature tours.
  5. Fix data quality visibly. Clean up the records users touch most and communicate the improvement, because nothing builds confidence faster than reports that finally reconcile.
  6. Provide fast, expert support at the moments that matter. On-demand access to specialists during registration, census, and aid disbursement prevents small frustrations from hardening into avoidance.

Improving the front-end experience compounds every one of these efforts. Investing in Constituent Experience Services, streamlining the screens and self-service flows that students and staff see most, reduces the effort required to do the right thing, which is the surest way to make a new system stick.

‍

How do you measure and sustain adoption?

You can't improve what you don't track, and adoption is measurable. Move beyond login counts to metrics that reflect genuine usage: percentage of transactions completed in-system versus by workaround, error and rework rates, self-service utilization, and time-to-complete for high-volume tasks. Set a baseline before major pushes and review the numbers with department leaders monthly, tying improvements to outcomes leaders already care about: faster registration, fewer redundant handoffs, cleaner reporting. Sustaining momentum means budgeting for ongoing enablement rather than assuming adoption holds on its own; planned, ongoing expertise can keep optimization going long after the initial project team departs. Institutions running deep Ellucian environments like Banner especially benefit from continuous tuning, because each academic cycle surfaces new edge cases that either reinforce or undermine user trust.

Adoption is ultimately a leadership discipline. Name: What should we ask before renewing our student system contract
Forefront Content:
Renewing your student information system is one of the highest-stakes decisions your institution makes, yet it often happens on autopilot, weeks before the deadline, when your leverage is lowest. The platform touches admissions, registration, financial aid, billing, and the entire student experience, so weak terms can lock in years of cost and friction. Knowing what should we ask before renewing our student system contract turns a routine procurement step into a genuine strategic evaluation. The questions below help you walk into the conversation informed, aligned, and ready to negotiate from strength.

‍

What is your student system really costing you, and why?

Start with total cost of ownership, not the invoice line you already recognize. The sticker price rarely reflects what the system actually consumes across a fiscal year, and that gap is easy to miss when renewal paperwork arrives on a deadline. Before you talk renewal terms, reconstruct the full picture:

  • Core licensing and annual maintenance or subscription fees
  • Hosting, infrastructure, and any premium environment charges
  • Custom development, third-party integrations, and middleware upkeep
  • Professional services and change orders billed outside the base contract
  • Internal staff hours spent on workarounds, manual reconciliation, and support tickets

When you total those honestly, many institutions find the "renewal price" is only part of true annual spend. That full number, not the quoted figure, is what you're really re-committing to. For a deeper dive into what you're actually paying, see how do we know if our student system is delivering ROI

‍

Are you actually using what you're paying for?

A contract renewal is the ideal moment for an honest utilization audit. Many campuses pay for modules, seats, and capabilities that were purchased with good intentions and never fully adopted. Pull the usage data: which functions are live, which are shelfware, and where staff have quietly built parallel spreadsheets because the system was too clunky to trust. This is where portfolio rationalization pays off, identifying redundancies between your SIS and adjacent tools you're also funding. If two systems both handle constituent communication or reporting, you may be paying twice for the same outcome. Renewing without this review means renewing your waste along with your value. For a comprehensive approach to this audit, explore how to audit our higher education tech stack

‍

What happens if you switch instead of renew?

Every renewal question is really a "renew versus replace" question, and you can't negotiate credibly without a real answer. Switching a student system is expensive, disruptive, and multi-year: data migration, retraining, and re-integration alone can consume a full cycle. But assuming it's "too hard to move" weakens your position at the table. Build a defensible switching-cost estimate and a realistic timeline for one credible alternative. Even if you fully intend to stay, a documented walk-away position changes the entire dynamic. Conversations go differently when both sides know you've done the math.

‍

How do you strengthen your position before signing?

Once you understand cost, usage, and alternatives, translate that into specific contractual asks. The best time to secure protections is before you re-sign, never after. Prioritize these in order:

  1. Price protection: cap annual increases and eliminate surprise escalators tied to enrollment or "usage."
  2. Service levels: enforceable SLAs for uptime, support response, and issue resolution, with meaningful remedies.
  3. Data ownership and exit rights: guaranteed access to your data in a usable format, plus reasonable transition assistance if you eventually leave.
  4. Security and compliance: documented alignment with FERPA, NIST, ISO 27001, and applicable privacy regulations, written into the agreement, not implied.
  5. Roadmap commitments: clarity on what's actually funded and coming, so you know how long your current product will be supported.

Each of these is negotiable. Institutions rarely ask, which is precisely why they rarely receive.

‍

Who needs to weigh in before you commit?

The final question is about governance, not procurement. A renewal signed by IT alone, or by finance chasing a deadline, almost always misses something the registrar, provost, or student-facing staff would have flagged. Bring the right voices to the table early: technology, records, financial aid, finance, and the people who live in the system daily. Strong IT governance means this decision reflects institutional strategy, not one office's convenience. This is also where outside perspective earns its keep. Because our consultants are former registrars, CIOs, and higher ed technology leaders who've sat in your chair, they know which commitments hold up in practice and which clauses deserve a second look. Whether through a focused advisory session or ongoing support that stays through negotiation, an independent read on your Banner, Colleague, or Anthology Student agreement helps you separate genuine value from renewal-cycle pressure.

A renewal you interrogate is a renewal you control. If your contract deadline is approaching and you want a seasoned second opinion before you sign, bring your agreement to our higher ed advisors and turn the negotiation in your favor.

Name: How do universities typically measure the success of working with an independent IT advisor?
Forefront Content:
Bringing in an outside IT advisor is a meaningful investment, and higher ed leaders rightly want proof that the engagement paid off. Yet "success" can look very different depending on whether you're a CIO chasing cost efficiency, a registrar untangling a student information system, or a president guarding the budget. The institutions that get the most value treat measurement as a discipline, not an afterthought. How do universities typically measure the success of working with an independent IT advisor? It starts with agreeing on what a win actually looks like.

‍

What "success" really means in an IT advisory engagement

Before any dashboard or scorecard, there has to be a shared definition of the outcome. On most campuses, an advisor is brought in to solve a specific, painful problem: a stalled ERP migration, redundant systems draining the budget, a governance vacuum, or a student experience that generates too many help-desk tickets. Success, then, is measured against the gap the engagement was hired to close, not against generic industry benchmarks. This is where a consultant who has actually sat in the registrar's or CIO's chair earns their keep, because they help leadership frame realistic, defensible goals rather than aspirational ones. The clearest engagements name the destination on day one so everyone can tell when they've arrived.

‍

The metrics universities use most often

Once the goal is defined, most institutions track a mix of hard and operational metrics. The way universities gauge the success of an independent IT advisor usually comes down to a handful of measurable signals:

  • Cost impact: dollars saved through portfolio rationalization, eliminated software redundancies, renegotiated licensing, or avoided implementation overruns.
  • Delivery against scope: whether the project landed on time, on budget, and against the specific deliverables written into the statement of work.
  • System performance and stability: fewer outages, faster integrations, cleaner data flows across Ellucian and connected platforms.
  • Adoption and utilization: are faculty, staff, and students actually using the systems the advisor helped optimize?
  • Student and constituent experience: reduced friction in registration, financial aid, and advising, often measured through satisfaction surveys and support-ticket volume.
  • Security and compliance posture: measurable progress toward FERPA, NIST, or ISO 27001 alignment and closure of audit findings.

Hard numbers give leadership something concrete to report to the board, which is why cost and delivery metrics tend to dominate the conversation.

‍

How to define success before the engagement begins

The universities that struggle to prove value are almost always the ones that never agreed on what value meant. To avoid that, strong measurement is built into the engagement up front:

  1. Diagnose the baseline. Document current costs, timelines, error rates, or satisfaction scores so you have something to compare against later.
  2. Set two or three primary KPIs. Resist the urge to track everything; pick the metrics that map directly to the problem being solved.
  3. Tie milestones to the timeline and budget. Break the engagement into checkpoints with clear deliverables, so progress is visible long before the final report.
  4. Assign ownership. Name who on campus is accountable for each metric, so measurement continues after the advisor's work is done.
  5. Schedule the review cadence. Agree on when and how results will be evaluated: monthly, per milestone, or at project close.

Whether the relationship is a scoped advisory project or ongoing support, this structure keeps both sides honest and makes the eventual verdict obvious rather than debatable.

‍

The qualitative signals that matter just as much

Not everything worth measuring fits neatly in a spreadsheet. Some of the most durable returns show up as capabilities the institution didn't have before. Did the engagement leave your team more confident and self-sufficient, or dependent on the consultant? Effective advisors bridge the gap between strategy and execution while transferring knowledge, so internal staff can sustain the gains. Look for maturing IT and data governance, stronger decision-making frameworks, and leaders who now ask sharper questions. A good sign is when campus stakeholders who were skeptical at the outset start defending the changes themselves. These softer indicators often predict long-term success better than any single quarter's cost savings, because they signal that the institution's underlying capacity, not just one project, has genuinely improved.

Name: What qualifications or experience should a university look for when selecting an independent IT advisor?
Forefront Content:
Bringing in outside help for a major systems decision can spare a campus years of frustration, or quietly add to it. The difference almost always comes down to who you hire. What qualifications or experience should a university look for when selecting an independent IT advisor? In short, someone who understands higher education from the inside, knows your technology intimately, and can carry a recommendation all the way through to a working result.

‍

They should have real higher education experience

The strongest advisors aren't career consultants who studied higher education from a distance. They've lived it. Prioritize people who have sat in the chairs your team occupies: former registrars who managed enrollment and records at scale, CIOs who owned a campus technology roadmap, and higher ed technology leaders who launched platforms under genuine budget and political pressure. That insider perspective matters because higher education runs on constraints outsiders rarely appreciate: shared governance, accreditation timelines, academic calendars, and the reality that a single misconfigured workflow can stall thousands of student records. An advisor who has walked in your shoes will diagnose faster, anticipate resistance, and translate technical options into decisions your provost and board can act on.

‍

They should know your technology ecosystem deeply

Broad IT credentials are not the same as fluency in the systems your institution actually runs. When you weigh what experience to prioritize in an independent IT consultant, look for demonstrated depth in your specific stack rather than generalist familiarity. If your student information system is Ellucian Banner, Colleague, or Anthology Student, your advisor should be able to speak to configuration, integration, and reporting nuances without a ramp-up period. Ask for:

  • Hands-on project history with your core platforms, not just vendor certifications
  • Experience integrating those systems with third-party tools and data pipelines
  • A track record of optimizing existing investments before recommending net-new spend
  • Familiarity with reporting and analytics needs across the registrar, finance, and advising offices

Deep ecosystem knowledge is what separates advice that sounds good in a slide deck from advice that survives contact with your production environment. For context on the complexity of these integrations, see Are there any risks or challenges associated with enabling more integrations and automation within our existing SIS platform?

‍

They should bridge strategy and execution

Plenty of firms will hand you a strategy and step back before anyone has to implement it. The qualifications that matter most when choosing an outside technology advisor include the ability to do both: set direction and help deliver it. Look for someone who can lead an executive-level roadmap or portfolio rationalization exercise, then work alongside your staff to actually stand up the change. Flexible engagement models are a strong signal here: project-based advisory for a defined assessment, on-demand access for a single thorny question, and ongoing support when you need planned capacity for months at a time. That range means you buy exactly the depth of help the moment requires, with clear timelines, budgets, and deliverables rather than an open-ended retainer.

‍

Governance, security, and compliance fluency

A qualified advisor treats governance and security as first-class concerns, not afterthoughts. Universities hold some of the most sensitive data any organization manages, including student records, financial aid, health information, and research, so your advisor should be conversant in the frameworks that protect it. Confirm working knowledge of FERPA, along with CCPA and GDPR where applicable, and alignment with recognized standards such as NIST and ISO 27001. Just as important, they should help you strengthen IT and data governance so decisions, ownership, and access controls are documented and durable after the engagement ends. Security fluency is one of the clearest markers of a senior, credible advisor.

‍

Questions to ask before you commit

Before you sign, put candidates through a short, honest vetting process:

1. Have you personally held a role inside a college or university, and in what capacity?

2. Can you show specific, recent work with our exact systems and a comparable institution?

3. How do you move from recommendation to implementation, and will the same people stay involved?

4. What engagement models do you offer, and how are scope, timeline, and cost defined?

5. How do you handle data governance, security, and compliance in your delivery?

6. What measurable outcomes, such as reduced redundancy, lower cost, or a better student experience, have you delivered before?

The answers reveal quickly whether you're hiring a genuine practitioner or a polished generalist. For a broader understanding of what advisors bring to the table, explore what does an independent IT advisor do for universities

Choosing well protects your budget, your timeline, and the students who ultimately feel every technology decision you make. Name: What does an independent IT advisor do for universities
Forefront Content:
Higher education now runs on a sprawling stack of student information systems, learning platforms, data warehouses, and cloud contracts, and most leadership teams are expected to manage all of it while also running an institution. When the stakes are a multi-year ERP migration or a major vendor renewal, an outside expert with no product to sell can be the difference between a confident decision and an expensive guess. That's where independent technology advisory comes in. This guide explains the role in plain terms so you can decide whether your institution needs one.

‍

What does an independent IT advisor do for universities?

At its core, what does an independent IT advisor do for universities comes down to one thing: providing objective, experienced guidance that isn't tied to selling any particular product. An advisor evaluates your current environment, clarifies where you're spending money and effort, and recommends a path forward that serves the institution, not a software license. In practice, that work usually includes:

  • Assessing systems and processes, from your SIS and ERP to the manual workarounds staff quietly rely on every day.
  • Advising on major decisions, including platform selection, contract negotiation, migration timing, and build-versus-buy questions.
  • Designing a roadmap with realistic sequencing, budget ranges, and risk mitigation.
  • Strengthening governance, so technology and data decisions follow a repeatable, accountable process instead of ad hoc politics.
  • Filling capability gaps with hands-on execution when your team is stretched thin.

The best advisors have sat in your chair as registrars, CIOs, and higher ed technology leaders, so they read your challenges from the inside rather than from a slide deck.

‍

Why do universities bring in an independent IT advisor?

Universities rarely lack smart people; they lack bandwidth, neutrality, and specialized depth at the exact moment a big decision lands. An independent voice solves all three. Because the advisor is vendor-neutral, their recommendation on whether to renew, replace, or optimize a platform carries no hidden incentive. Because the engagement is scoped and temporary, you get senior expertise without adding a permanent line to the budget. And because these advisors specialize, they've already navigated the migration, integration, or audit you're facing for the first time.

There's also a candor factor. Internal teams may hesitate to challenge a beloved system or a powerful stakeholder. An outside advisor can say what needs saying, backed by evidence, and give leadership the political cover to act on it.

‍

Where an independent university IT advisor adds the most value

Not every project needs outside help, but a few situations reliably benefit from it:

  1. ERP and SIS modernization. Independent oversight helps multi-year modernization efforts stay on track, separate from the teams doing the implementation. Deep familiarity with the Ellucian ecosystem, including Banner and Colleague, turns a chaotic migration into a sequenced plan with fewer surprises.
  2. System integration. Advisors map how your platforms exchange data, eliminate brittle point-to-point connections, and reduce the redundancies that inflate cost and error rates. For deeper context on integration challenges, see Are there any risks or challenges associated with enabling more integrations and automation within our existing SIS platform?
  3. Portfolio rationalization. They inventory overlapping tools and licenses, then recommend what to consolidate, retire, or renegotiate. Learn more about this approach in What strategies can institutions use to reduce the financial impact of software sprawl without disrupting essential services?
  4. Governance and cybersecurity. They establish IT and data governance and align your posture with frameworks like NIST, ISO 27001, and FERPA.
  5. Student and constituent experience. They connect back-office fixes to the outcomes leadership actually cares about: smoother enrollment, faster service, better retention.

‍

How is an independent advisor different from a vendor or a new hire?

A vendor's team knows its own products deeply, but its recommendations naturally center on that catalog. A full-time hire takes months to recruit, represents a long-term salary commitment, and may still lack the exact specialty you need for a one-time initiative. An independent advisor sits between those extremes: senior enough to guide the C-suite, flexible enough to engage for a defined project, and unbiased enough to tell you the uncomfortable truth. Engagements can flex from a single strategic assessment to ongoing support that bridges the gap between strategy and execution, so you scale expertise up or down as the work demands, with clear timelines, budgets, and deliverables.

‍

When should your institution engage one?

Watch for the signals. You're renewing or replacing a core system. Integrations keep breaking and no one fully owns them. Costs are climbing but no one can explain why. A security audit or compliance deadline is looming. Leadership can't get a straight, unbiased answer on a major technology bet. Any one of these is reason enough to bring in outside perspective; two or three together mean you're likely already paying for the problem in wasted time and money.

Name: Top higher education consulting firms
Forefront Content:
Choosing a consulting partner is one of the highest-leverage decisions a college or university can make, and one of the easiest to get wrong. The market is crowded with generalist advisory shops, staffing agencies wearing consulting labels, and technology resellers whose recommendations tend to point back to their own products. For business decision-makers on campus, the real challenge isn't finding a firm; it's separating the ones who understand the mechanics of enrollment, financial aid, student records, and institutional technology from the ones who learned about them on your dime. This guide breaks down what the Top higher education consulting firms actually deliver, how they differ, and how to evaluate them so your investment produces measurable results rather than a binder of recommendations no one implements.

‍

What higher education consulting firms do

At their best, higher education consulting firms help institutions solve problems that internal teams either don't have the bandwidth to tackle or don't have the specialized expertise to close on their own. That work spans a wide spectrum. Some engagements are strategic: rethinking a portfolio of technology investments, designing an IT or data governance model, or building a multi-year roadmap for modernizing student-facing systems. Others are deeply operational: untangling a stalled ERP implementation, cleaning up integrations that keep breaking, or standing up reporting that gives leadership a single, trustworthy view of the numbers.

The common thread is that these firms exist to translate ambition into execution. A provost may want to improve retention. A CFO may want to reduce the number of overlapping software licenses. A CIO may need to harden the institution's security posture before the next audit. Consulting firms bring the methodology, the outside perspective, and the specialized hands to move those goals from conversation to completed work. The strongest partners don't just diagnose problems. They stay long enough to fix them, transfer knowledge to your team, and leave the institution more capable than they found it.

It helps to understand the typical engagement models you'll encounter:

  • Project-based advisory, where a firm scopes a defined deliverable with a fixed timeline and budget, such as an assessment, a roadmap, or a system optimization.
  • Fractional or embedded support, where senior expertise plugs into your organization on a part-time or ongoing basis to fill a leadership gap or accelerate a program.
  • On-demand or structured services, where you access specialized help for discrete needs without committing to a long engagement.

The best firms offer more than one of these so the model can flex to the problem instead of forcing every problem into the same billing structure.

‍

What separates the top firms from the rest

Search "higher education consulting" and you'll get hundreds of options. What actually distinguishes the leaders is rarely the length of their capabilities list. It's the depth behind it. When institutions tell us where past engagements went sideways, the same themes surface: consultants who never worked inside a college, recommendations that ignored operational reality, and strategies that were never built to be implemented. The firms worth your budget avoid those failures by design.

A few signals reliably separate the strongest higher education consultants from the rest of the field:

  • Practitioner pedigree. The most credible firms are staffed by former registrars, CIOs, financial aid directors, and higher ed technology executives, people who have actually run the offices they now advise. That insider perspective compresses the learning curve and produces recommendations grounded in how campuses really operate.
  • Both strategy and execution under one roof. Many firms will hand you a plan; far fewer will help you build it. The ability to bridge the gap between strategy and execution is one of the clearest markers of a top-tier partner.
  • Genuine specialization. Generalists spread thin across every vertical rarely match the value of firms with deep expertise in the specific systems and ecosystems higher education runs on.
  • Transparent, tailored delivery. Leading firms commit to specific timelines, budgets, and deliverables rather than open-ended engagements that quietly expand.
  • A serious governance and security posture. With FERPA, CCPA, GDPR, and frameworks like NIST and ISO 27001 in play, the best partners treat data protection as a baseline, not an afterthought.

When you weigh options among the top higher education consulting firms, these attributes matter far more than brand recognition or a polished pitch deck. A firm that has walked in your shoes will spot risks a generalist misses, and will design around the constraints your team lives with every day.

‍

Core services the best firms deliver

The strongest firms cover a recognizable set of service areas, and understanding that landscape helps you match a partner to your actual need rather than buying whatever they happen to sell. Broadly, the work falls into a few categories.

Platform and ERP expertise

Most institutions run their core operations on a small number of major platforms, and specialized consulting exists for each. According to ListEdTech's January 2025 market data, Ellucian Banner holds the largest share of the North American higher ed SIS market at 24 percent, followed by Ellucian Colleague. With Ellucian's completed acquisition of Anthology's SIS and ERP business at the end of 2025, Anthology Student institutions are now part of the same ecosystem. Firms with deep Ellucian experience support implementations, upgrades, and optimizations across all three. If a firm claims platform expertise, ask how many implementations their consultants have personally led and whether they've held roles that depended on those systems day to day. Surface-level familiarity is easy to fake; operational fluency isn't.

‍

Integration and data

As campuses accumulate dozens of applications, the connective tissue between them becomes a primary source of both risk and opportunity. Strong firms offer integration services that make disparate systems talk to each other reliably, along with reporting and analytics services that turn scattered data into decisions leadership can trust. This matters even more after a SaaS migration, when data flows that worked for years suddenly need to be rebuilt. When your admissions system, SIS, and finance platform each tell a slightly different story, no amount of strategy fixes the underlying data problem. Integration and governance do.

‍

Optimization, managed services, and governance

Beyond initial implementations, the highest-value work often lives in ongoing improvement. Optimization services help institutions get more value out of systems they already own by reducing redundancies, streamlining processes, and controlling cost. Managed services provide sustained operational support so internal teams can focus on mission-critical priorities rather than firefighting. And mature IT governance and data governance frameworks give leadership the structure to make consistent, defensible decisions about technology and information over time.

‍

Strategy, coaching, and change

Technology never fails in a vacuum; it fails when people, process, and politics aren't aligned. That's why the best firms pair technical delivery with services like portfolio rationalization, executive coaching, cybersecurity, and change management. A system rollout that ignores adoption is a system rollout that stalls. Firms that understand this build the human side of change into every engagement rather than treating it as an optional add-on.

You won't need all of these at once. The point is to choose a partner whose depth matches the problem in front of you, and whose range means they can keep helping as your priorities evolve.

‍

Why practitioner-led consulting changes the outcome

There's a meaningful difference between a consultant who has read about the registrar's office and one who has run it through a catalog conversion, a commencement crunch, and three years of shifting compliance requirements. That difference shows up in the quality of the recommendations and, more importantly, in whether they survive contact with reality.

Consider a common scenario. An institution wants to consolidate overlapping software and reduce licensing spend. A generalist firm benchmarks your tools against a rubric and produces a rationalization plan that looks clean on paper. A practitioner-led firm does the same analysis, but also knows that the "redundant" advising tool the plan flags for removal is the one three departments actually depend on for early-alert workflows, and that removing it without a migration path would hurt the retention numbers the provost cares about. That contextual judgment is the value. It's the difference between a plan that gets shelved and one that gets executed.

This is where flexible delivery models earn their keep. Some institutions need a defined project with a clear scope and end date. Others need a senior expert for a focused, time-boxed problem without standing up a full engagement. And some need experienced consultants working alongside their team on an ongoing basis, which is where a skills-based managed services model like Doctums Extend fits. The best firms let the engagement model follow the problem, offering fractional or full-time resources with the flexibility your institution actually needs rather than forcing every relationship into a single template.

Practitioner-led delivery also changes the tenor of the relationship. When your consultant has sat in your chair, conversations move faster, assumptions get challenged productively, and knowledge transfers naturally. You're not educating an outsider. You're working with a peer who has solved this problem at other campuses.

‍

How to evaluate and choose the right firm

Name: Is Your Team Ready for 1098-T Season? Here's Your Step-by-Step Guide.
Forefront Content:
When was the last time your 1098-T season ended without a late-January scramble? 

If the answer is "never," you're not alone. Over many 1098-T seasons, the thing I've seen cause the most stress isn't a technical mistake. It's waiting until the end of January, when there's no time left to test. This year the IRS is changing how institutions file, so I put together this guide to help your team get ahead of it, step by step.

‍

Step 1: Understand what's different this year

For years, institutions have filed their 1098-Ts electronically through the IRS's FIRE system. That system is being retired. The IRS lists November 19, 2026, at 3 p.m. ET as the last day to file information returns through FIRE. Starting with the 2027 filing season, the Information Returns Intake System (IRIS) will be the only way to file electronically.

Here's what that means for your team:

  • You'll need a new TCC code. Filing through IRIS requires its own Transmitter Control Code (TCC). Your FIRE TCC won't carry over.
  • Request it now. It can take up to 45 days to receive a new TCC, so apply for your IRIS TCC as early as you can. If you request it in mid-October, it should arrive by the end of November with room to spare. If you wait until January, you may not have it in time.
  • This applies to almost everyone. Institutions with 10 or more information returns are required to file electronically, so for most schools, IRIS isn't optional.

You may see other dates on IRS pages for updating existing FIRE applications. To be safe, plan around November 19. For the full process, see the IRS guide to filing with IRIS.

‍

Step 2: Mark these dates on your calendar

  • December 31, 2026: Deadline to make a good faith effort to collect any missing Social Security numbers or taxpayer identification numbers (SSN/TIN) from students. The IRS instructions for Form 1098-T explain what that effort involves.
  • February 1, 2027: January 31 falls on a Sunday this year, so 1098-Ts sent by mail must be postmarked by February 1 at the latest.
  • March 31, 2027: Your electronic 1098-T file is due to the IRS via IRIS.

‍

Step 3: Before December, get the pieces in place

  • If you use a third party to process your 1098-Ts, confirm that the contract is in place and that you've agreed on a plan and a timeline.
  • If you process in house, ask students early how they'd like to receive their form. Electronic delivery requires student consent, so the earlier you ask, the fewer forms you'll need to mail.
  • Order your envelopes now. This is the item I see slip most often. By late January, every business is printing and mailing tax forms, and expediting an order costs money you didn't plan to spend.
  • Review what you're telling students, including your website, and update anything that changed for the new year.

‍

Step 4: In January, test before you file

Testing is where a smooth season gets built. Focus on two things.

Check your codes. Any new charge, payment, or financial aid codes created during the year need to be mapped to the right boxes on the form. A code set up mid-year for a new fee or program is easy to miss, and a single unmapped code can affect every student it touches.

Test a wide range of student scenarios, including:

  • Charges posted in 2026 for courses that start between January 1 and March 31, 2027
  • Students living in campus housing
  • Different student populations
  • Different ways of paying: personal payments, financial aid (scholarships, grants, and loans), and third-party payments

A lesson learned: the hardest lesson I've learned came from a change the IRS made several years ago. Institutions used to report the amount charged during the calendar year, in Box 2. Starting with tax year 2018, they had to report payments received during the calendar year, in Box 1. Because schools typically bill for the spring term in December, a student can pay for spring classes in one tax year and attend them in the next. That crossover shows up on the form. Account for it when you review your calculations, and explain it to students before the questions start coming in.

‍

Step 5: Plan for the people, not just the forms

Much of the 1098-T process often lives in one or two people's heads. When the person who has always handled it moves on, someone new in Student Accounts inherits a process with tight deadlines and very little room for trial and error. A written timeline and a checklist like this one are often what keep the season on track. We wrote more about that kind of knowledge gap in Higher Ed's Real IT Shortage Isn't People. It's What They Take With Them.

‍

We don't produce 1098-T forms, and we're not tax experts. Where we help is the process around them. We work with institutions on an as-needed basis to set up and improve how 1098-T season runs, so it creates less anxiety year after year. That often means helping a new Student Accounts staff member work through the process for the first time, or reviewing setup before testing begins.

Artificial intelligence now adds a different variable. The question is no longer only where the SIS lives or how it gets updated. The major technology ecosystems are starting to build data, analytics, automation, AI, and agents around their transactional systems. The traditional System of Record is beginning to aspire to become a System of Intelligence as well. And that deserves a strategic conversation.

‍

Many Good Decisions Can Add Up to One We Never Made

A university may reasonably decide to move its SIS to SaaS. Later, it may adopt the same vendor’s data platform. Then its analytics solution. Then its AI capabilities. And finally, its agents. Each decision, evaluated on its own, can make sense. Integration reduces complexity, simplifies security, and lowers the effort required to add new capabilities. But the cumulative result is worth a closer look. Did the institution explicitly decide to concentrate its system of record, its data, its processes, its analytics, and a significant part of its intelligence in a single ecosystem? Or did it get there through a sequence of individual decisions, each one reasonable? The difference matters.

‍

Future Dependency Can Be Built on Convenience

We have traditionally associated vendor lock-in with contracts, proprietary technologies, or high migration costs. AI may introduce a far subtler form of dependency: ease. Imagine a university needs to develop an agent to support student retention. One option is already connected to its data, integrated with its systems, approved by security, and part of its existing technology ecosystem. The other requires selecting a vendor, contracting with it, enabling APIs, resolving integrations, completing a cybersecurity review, testing, and training users. The first option will likely have an enormous advantage, not necessarily because it is better, but because it has less friction. The vendor doesn’t need to prevent the university from using other solutions. It may be enough to make staying within its ecosystem extraordinarily easy.

‍

The Question Isn’t SaaS or No SaaS

SaaS represents a real technological evolution and offers significant advantages for many institutions. Nor is there any reason to assume that building AI capabilities in-house will always be the better path. In many cases, using the intelligence built in by major vendors will be more efficient, more secure, and more financially reasonable. The real discussion is a different one. What capabilities does a university want to delegate, and which ones does it need to keep under its own control? Data. Integrations. Processes. Institutional rules. Intelligence models. Agents. The ability to adopt future solutions. There is no universal answer. But there should be a conscious decision.

‍

The Age of the Investment Matters Too

This conversation is especially relevant for institutions that have recently made major investments in their current platforms. A university that has been using its SIS for many years may see a new platform as the natural evolution of an asset whose initial investment has already paid off. For one that finished an implementation two or three years ago, the same proposal can mean something entirely different. It isn’t facing just a technology decision. It has to justify a new investment, protect the value of the previous one, manage internal expectations, rebuild credibility with those who took part in the original decision, and, at the same time, make decisions about an artificial intelligence whose future development still carries significant uncertainty. Both universities may run the same SIS today, but they are not facing the same decision.

‍

Maybe We Need to Change the Question

For a long time, we have asked: What is the best technology for our university? Perhaps we should add a second question: What decisions do we want to still be able to make five years from now? This introduces a particularly relevant concept: option value. A good technology architecture shouldn’t be judged only by the functionality it provides today. It should also be judged by how many alternatives it preserves for tomorrow. Will we be able to use our data independently? Integrate new solutions? Bring in our own or third-party models and agents? Replace one component without rebuilding the entire ecosystem? Take advantage of an innovation that doesn’t exist yet? In a relatively stable technology environment, these questions might have seemed secondary. At the current pace of artificial intelligence, they are becoming strategic.

‍

Preserving the Ability to Choose

At Doctums, we believe the next technology conversation in higher education shouldn’t be limited to choosing between on-premise and SaaS, between one vendor and another, or between building and buying artificial intelligence. It should help us understand what institutional architecture we are building as a result of those decisions. Because adopting a technology doesn’t only mean acquiring the capabilities it offers today. It can also expand, or narrow, the options we will have tomorrow. That is why one of the most important responsibilities for those of us who support universities through their technology transformation may be helping preserve something that rarely appears in an RFP: their future ability to choose. Today’s best technology decision shouldn’t necessarily be the one that promises to solve everything. It should also be the one that allows us to keep making good decisions when the future turns out different from what we imagine today.

‍

Written by Rodolfo González Gatica

Name: Before You Choose a New ERP, Decide What Success Looks Like.
Forefront Content:
Written by Doctums Staff

Ask an IT leader in higher education whether their institution will move its ERP to SaaS, and the honest answer is increasingly “when,” not “if.” Most of the institutions we work with are somewhere between early planning and active transition. That part is rarely in question anymore.

‍

What is still in question is how they’ll get there, and whether the institution will actually run better on the other side. That outcome is mostly decided before a single system is selected.

Why the move is coming either way

The pressure on institutions isn’t coming from one direction. Maintaining a server room is expensive, and getting funding approved on a reasonable replacement cycle gets harder every budget season. Keeping student and employee data on local servers carries real risk, and most institutions can’t hire the security expertise to manage it alone. Meanwhile, more and more higher ed software is no longer sold for local installation at all.

‍

“Very few institutions will be able to avoid moving to SaaS. Even the ones still in planning will eventually have to make the leap, whether they decide to change systems or their current system changes how it’s licensed and supported.”

— Connie Atchley, Senior Consultant, Doctums

‍

The scale of the work has changed too.

‍

“Gone are the days when an IT team managed ten servers. Today they’re keeping hundreds of physical and virtual machines patched and secure, and finding qualified people to do that keeps getting harder.”

— Sulema Cabrera, Senior Consultant, Doctums

‍

That talent gap isn’t new, and it isn’t only about headcount. We wrote about what institutions actually lose when experienced IT staff move on.

‍

What modernization actually means

When an institution tells us it wants to modernize, it usually means one of two things: moving to SaaS and needing a trusted advisor along the way, or getting more out of the student information system it already has. Either way, the conversation starts in the same place.

‍

“Modernization isn’t simply about moving from an on-premises system to the cloud. It’s about stepping back, understanding where an institution is today, and figuring out how technology, processes, and people can work together to get where it wants to go. Our goal is to help institutions make decisions that set them up for the long term, not just get them through a migration.”

— Heather Harrison, Director of Advisory Services, Doctums

‍

Why the system is rarely the problem

EDUCAUSE research on ERP implementations in higher education makes a point institutions often learn too late: go-live shouldn’t be the measure of success. Customizations and the design of future business processes are among the biggest hurdles, and each institution has to define what success means for itself. In our experience, the software is rarely what holds a project back.

‍

The reason is usually what institutions bring with them. Years of workarounds, custom modifications, and processes that exist because “that’s how we’ve always done it” don’t disappear in a new system. Cloud ERP leaves less room for deep customization, which forces institutions to reconcile workflows that never matched across departments in the first place, as ERP Today has reported. If those differences aren’t addressed early, they surface mid-project, when they’re most expensive to fix.

‍

We’ve seen the same pattern in how community colleges are handling outcomes-based funding: a decade of workarounds stays invisible until something forces the data to hold up.

‍

What to assess before you select

None of this requires waiting until a contract is signed. The most valuable work happens before selection, and it starts with an honest look at the current state.

‍

How work actually gets done today. 

That means existing workflows, data quality, integrations, and institutional requirements, not how the system is supposed to work in theory.

‍

What should change and what should carry forward.

“If legacy processes get replicated without anyone asking why they exist, institutions end up carrying the same inefficiencies and complexity into the new ERP. The honest conversation about what should change versus what should carry forward is the one that gets skipped most.”

— Heather Harrison, Director of Advisory Services, Doctums

‍

Where the friction is.

“Before anything else, we ask what’s working and what isn’t. Where are functional areas feeling the pain? What parts of the system aren’t being used today that could make people’s work easier? And can this modernization be tied directly to the institution’s strategic goals?”

— Sulema Cabrera, Senior Consultant, Doctums

‍

The reports you can’t live without. 

Every institution has reports it depends on for compliance, leadership, and day-to-day decisions. Building an inventory of must-have reports, and deciding whether the current reporting platform stays or goes, prevents some of the most disruptive surprises after go-live.

‍

Institutions that do this work first don’t just choose better. They choose with a clear definition of what success looks like, which is the only way to know later whether they got there.

‍

Where an independent advisor helps

As an independent higher education consulting firm, Doctums brings decades of experience with ERP and SIS platforms, and no system to sell. 

‍

“Before selection, we help institutions build the criteria they’ll use to evaluate vendors, and we can facilitate the decision as a neutral party. Because we’ve worked with these systems and these institutions for so long, we can bring insight into the conversation that wouldn’t otherwise be in the room.”

— Connie Atchley, Senior Consultant, Doctums

‍

From there, we support institutions through implementation and well after go-live.

‍

Go-live is not the finish line

Modernization will look different for every institution, but the ones that get the most from it share one thing: they defined success before they defined the system. In our next piece, we’ll look at what happens once the system is chosen, and why the real timeline is set by the institution, not the technology.

‍

If your institution is starting to plan its move, or you’re not sure where to begin, that’s exactly the conversation we’re glad to have.

‍

Talk to our team.

Written by Doctums Staff
